Autoregressive Diffusion World Models for Off-Policy Evaluation of LLM Agents

Kaixuan Liu Affiliation: Emory University Email: kaixuan.liu@emory.edu    Guojun Xiong ††thanks: Correspondence to Guojun Xiong <gjxiong@sjtu.edu.cn>. Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University Email: gjxiong@sjtu.edu.cn    Weinan Zhang Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University Email: wnzhang@sjtu.edu.cn    Shengpu Tang Affiliation: Emory University Email: shengpu.tang@emory.edu
Abstract

Evaluating large language model (LLM) agents in multi-turn interactive environments is expensive and risky, as it requires online environment interaction. We propose Adwm (Autoregressive Diffusion World Model), an evaluation framework that estimates the performance of a new LLM agent policy purely from pre-collected trajectories. The core idea is to learn a latent diffusion world model that simulates how the environment responds to the evaluation policy, without ever executing it in the real environment. Existing diffusion-based OPE methods guide full trajectories in a single pass by jointly diffusing states and actions, an assumption that breaks down for LLM agents whose actions are discrete text that must be sampled from the policy after observing the environment. Unlike textual world models that generate each observation token by token, Adwm jointly denoises the complete next observation in latent space, enabling step-by-step rollouts where the world model and agent alternate in causal order. Crucially, the LLM agent under evaluation directly guides the diffusion generation at each step via a policy-conditioned score function, ensuring that simulated trajectories accurately reflect its decision-making patterns. Empirically, Adwm achieves accurate policy rankings and evaluation reliability across diverse multi-turn agent tasks, demonstrating its promise as a practical framework for offline LLM agent evaluation. Code is available at https://github.com/kaixuanliu-ai/ADWM.

1 Introduction

Large language model agents are increasingly deployed in multi-turn interactive environments, navigating websites, writing and executing code, and reasoning over long document contexts [41, 44, 21]. As these agents are trusted with higher-stakes tasks, evaluating a new agent policy before deployment becomes critical. Yet evaluation is expensive; every new agent must be executed live in the real environment, consuming API budget and potentially causing irreversible side effects.

Off-policy evaluation (OPE) addresses this challenge by estimating the value of a new agent from pre-collected offline data, without any further environment interaction. Importance sampling methods reweight offline trajectories by policy likelihood ratios [25, 28], but these weights grow exponentially with trajectory length, making the estimator impractical for multi-turn agentic settings. Value-based direct methods attempt to fit a value function on offline data [24, 31], but suffer from compounding bias when the evaluation policy differs substantially from the behavior policy. Doubly robust methods combine the two [7, 23], partially mitigating these issues but not resolving the fundamental difficulty of long-horizon distribution shift in high-dimensional text spaces.

Among direct methods, a more promising model-based alternative is to build a world model: learn the environment dynamics from offline data and simulate rollouts under the evaluation policy [11, 26]. In the agentic setting, this simulation must be autoregressive: each LLM action depends on the observation just received, so the world model and agent must alternate step by step in causal order. Autoregressive transformer-based world models [29] follow this structure naturally, but generate observations token by token, causing errors to accumulate within each step and compound further across steps, a critical failure mode for the long-horizon tasks that LLM agents face. Diffusion models offer a principled remedy: by jointly denoising the complete next observation, they remove the token-level error chain within each step [13, 5], and score-function guidance enables the evaluation policy to steer rollouts without retraining. However, existing diffusion-based methods for offline RL and OPE [17, 26, 9] were designed for continuous control, where states and actions are both real-valued vectors that can be jointly noised and denoised as a single tensor in one pass, with actions generated by the diffusion process itself and the evaluation policy entering only as a guidance signal. In LLM agent settings, this assumption fundamentally breaks down: actions are discrete text that must be sampled from the LLM after observing the environment and cannot participate in a joint continuous diffusion over trajectories. Generating full trajectories in a single pass therefore requires all LLM actions to be known before any observation is generated, a circular dependency that is irreconcilable with the step-by-step rollout that agentic evaluation demands.

We propose Adwm (Autoregressive Diffusion World Model), an offline evaluation framework for LLM agents that resolves this tension by instantiating the world model itself as a diffusion process (see Figure 1). The key insight is that the globally policy-guided trajectory law can be exactly factored into a sequence of single-step conditionals, each decomposing as a product of a prior, an action-posterior, and a policy continuation factor (Theorem 1). This product structure maps directly onto guided diffusion, with the evaluation policy steering every denoising step via its log-likelihood gradient. Because each next observation is denoised jointly, Adwm avoids the within-step token-level error chain, although transition errors may still propagate across steps. Adwm is trained entirely offline, and a new agent only requires fitting a lightweight adapter.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:
⊳\triangleright We derive the exact autoregressive single-step conditional induced by a policy-guided trajectory law, showing it decomposes into a principled three-factor product (Theorem 1).
⊳\triangleright We realize this decomposition as a guided diffusion process in a structured latent space, where the evaluation policy participates in every denoising step without retraining the world model.
⊳\triangleright We demonstrate empirically that Adwm correctly ranks evaluation policies across diverse LLM agent benchmarks, outperforming classic OPE baselines under realistic LLM importance ratios.

2 Related Work

Model-Based OPE.

Model-based OPE methods estimate policy value by learning a transition model from offline data and simulating rollouts under the evaluation policy [43, 42]. The core difficulty is compounding model error: small inaccuracies in the learned transition accumulate across steps, causing simulated trajectories to drift away from the true environment dynamics over long horizons [19, 35, 2]. Existing approaches mitigate this through pessimistic value penalties or conservative policy optimization [22], but these techniques were designed for low-dimensional continuous control and do not extend to free-form text observations. Beyond error accumulation, these methods provide no mechanism for conditioning the simulated rollout on the evaluation policy, so generated trajectories reflect the behavior distribution rather than what the evaluation policy would actually produce [36, 8]. Adwm addresses both issues: jointly denoising each next observation removes the token-level error chain within a step [18, 1], while the guided score function ensures every generated observation is conditioned on the evaluation policy.

Diffusion Models for World Modeling.

Diffusion models have emerged as powerful environment simulators that generate each transition through an iterative denoising process rather than token by token. Full-sequence models jointly generate entire trajectories [18, 1, 15], treating states and actions as a single jointly diffused tensor. This design precludes step-by-step rollout, as actions are produced by the diffusion process itself rather than sampled from an external policy. Score-based guidance [14] can steer such generation toward a target policy [26, 17], but inherits the same limitation: actions must be real-valued vectors that participate in the joint diffusion, an assumption that breaks down for LLM agents whose actions are discrete text sampled from the policy after observing the environment. Adwm resolves this by deriving an exact factored score that enables the evaluation policy to steer each denoising step autoregressively, without requiring actions to be part of the diffusion process. Autoregressive video diffusion models such as Diffusion Forcing [3] and Self Forcing [16] generate frames sequentially by assigning per-frame noise levels and by training on self-generated histories, respectively. These methods study sequential generation within a single diffusion model. Adwm instead alternates a diffusion world model with an external evaluation policy whose action is available only after it observes the current observation, so the interaction trajectory cannot be jointly diffused without violating causal order.

Textual World Models for LLM Agents.

LLMs themselves can act as world models that predict environment feedback in text. SURGE [27] studies LLMs as surrogate code executors, CWM [6] trains a code LLM on execution traces and agentic interactions, and RAP [12] uses an LLM world model for planning during reasoning. These simulators generate each observation token by token, so an early token error changes the prefix of all remaining tokens within the same environment step. Moreover, they target code execution, environment simulation, or online planning rather than OPE. Adwm learns from offline behavior trajectories, denoises the complete next-observation latent jointly, and estimates the value of a distinct evaluation policy without additional real-environment interaction.

3 Problem Formulation

3.1 Agentic Reinforcement Learning

We formulate agentic reinforcement learning as a sequential decision-making problem, modeled as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) ℳ=(𝒮,𝒜,𝒪,P,ℰ,r,μ,γ)\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{O},P,\mathcal{E},r,\mu,\gamma), where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the state space, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the action space, 𝒪\mathcal{O} is the observation space, P:𝒮×𝒜→Δ⁡(𝒮)P:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\Delta(\mathcal{S}) is the transition kernel, ℰ:𝒮→Δ⁡(𝒪)\mathcal{E}:\mathcal{S}\to\Delta(\mathcal{O}) is the emission distribution, r:𝒮×𝒜→ℝr:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R} is the reward function, μ∈Δ⁡(𝒮)\mu\in\Delta(\mathcal{S}) is the initial state distribution, and γ∈[0,1)\gamma\in[0,1) is the discount factor. Since the agent does not have direct access to sts_{t}, it instead receives a partial observation ot∼ℰ(⋅∣st)o_{t}\sim\mathcal{E}(\cdot\mid s_{t}) emitted by the environment. The agent interacts with the environment over TT turns. At each turn t∈{1,…,T}t\in\{1,\dots,T\}, the environment is in state st∈𝒮s_{t}\in\mathcal{S}, from which the agent receives observation ot∈𝒪o_{t}\in\mathcal{O} and selects an action at∼π(⋅∣ht)a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid h_{t}) based on the interaction history:

ht=(o1,a1,…,ot−1,at−1,ot).h_{t}=(o_{1},a_{1},\dots,o_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_{t}).

The environment then transitions to the next state st+1∼P(⋅∣st,at)s_{t+1}\sim P(\cdot\mid s_{t},a_{t}) and emits a reward rt=r⁡(st,at)r_{t}=r(s_{t},a_{t}). A complete trajectory τ=(o1,a1,r1,…,oT,aT,rT)\tau=(o_{1},a_{1},r_{1},\dots,o_{T},a_{T},r_{T}) has discounted return R⁡(τ)=∑t=1Tγt−1​rtR(\tau)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma^{t-1}r_{t}, and induces the trajectory distribution:

pπ(τ)=∫μ(s1)∏t=1Tℰ(ot∣st)π(at∣ht)P(st+1∣st,at)ds1:T+1.p_{\pi}(\tau)=\int\mu(s_{1})\prod_{t=1}^{T}\mathcal{E}(o_{t}\mid s_{t})\,\pi(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\,P(s_{t+1}\mid s_{t},a_{t})\,ds_{1:T+1}.

The value of policy π\pi is thus J⁡(π)=𝔼τ∼pπ​[R⁡(τ)]J(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_{\pi}}[R(\tau)]. For example, in WebShop [40], oto_{t} is the current web page together with the task instruction, the LLM reads hth_{t} and outputs a text action ata_{t} such as search[...] or click[buy now], and the environment returns the next page ot+1o_{t+1}, the reward rtr_{t}, and a termination signal. A logged episode annotated with this notation is given in Section F.11.

3.2 Off-Policy Evaluation for LLM Agents

We assume access to an offline dataset:

𝒟={τ(i)}i=1N,τ(i)∼pπb​(τ),\mathcal{D}=\{\tau^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N},\qquad\tau^{(i)}\sim p_{\pi_{b}}(\tau),

collected by a behavior policy πb\pi_{b}, which may correspond to a mixture of different LLM configurations and is treated as unknown. Given 𝒟\mathcal{D} and a target evaluation policy πe\pi_{e}, a language model distinct from πb\pi_{b} that maps observation history hth_{t} to a distribution over text actions, the goal of off-policy evaluation (OPE) is to estimate:

J⁡(πe)=𝔼τ∼pπe​[R⁡(τ)],J(\pi_{e})=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_{\pi_{e}}}[R(\tau)],

without executing πe\pi_{e} in the real environment. The core challenge is distribution shift: since pπb​(τ)≠pπe​(τ)p_{\pi_{b}}(\tau)\neq p_{\pi_{e}}(\tau), trajectories in 𝒟\mathcal{D} are not representative samples from pπep_{\pi_{e}}, and direct Monte Carlo estimation on 𝒟\mathcal{D} is severely biased. We address this challenge by learning a diffusion world model that simulates rollouts under πe\pi_{e} directly, bypassing the need for explicit density ratio estimation.

3.3 Denoising Diffusion Models

Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) [13] learn to approximate a target distribution q⁡(x)q(x) via two coupled Markov chains. The forward process gradually corrupts a clean sample x0∼q⁡(x)x^{0}\sim q(x) over KK steps:

xk=α¯k​x0+1−α¯k​ϵ,ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I),x^{k}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{k}}\,x^{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{k}}\,\epsilon,\qquad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I),

where {α¯k}k=1K\{\bar{\alpha}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} is a decreasing noise schedule with α¯K≈0\bar{\alpha}_{K}\approx 0. The reverse process learns to recover x0x^{0} from xKx^{K} by iteratively applying pθ​(xk−1∣xk)=𝒩⁡(xk−1,μθ​(xk,k),σk2​I)p_{\theta}(x^{k-1}\mid x^{k})=\mathcal{N}(x^{k-1};\,\mu_{\theta}(x^{k},k),\,\sigma_{k}^{2}I), where μθ\mu_{\theta} is parameterized via a noise prediction network ϵθ\epsilon_{\theta} trained by:

ℒ⁡(θ)=𝔼k,x0,ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)​[‖ϵ−ϵθ​(xk,k)‖2].\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{k,\,x^{0},\,\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)}\bigl[\,\|\epsilon-\epsilon_{\theta}(x^{k},k)\|^{2}\,\bigr].

Guided diffusion.

A trained diffusion model can be steered to sample from a conditional distribution p⁡(x∣y)p(x\mid y) without retraining, by incorporating a guidance signal yy into each denoising step [5]. Since the backward transition is well approximated by a Gaussian, p⁡(xk∣xk+1)≈𝒩⁡(μk,Σk)p(x^{k}\mid x^{k+1})\approx\mathcal{N}(\mu_{k},\Sigma_{k}), Bayes’ rule gives:

p⁡(xk∣xk+1,y)∝p⁡(xk∣xk+1)​p​(y∣xk).p(x^{k}\mid x^{k+1},y)\propto p(x^{k}\mid x^{k+1})\,p(y\mid x^{k}).

Applying a first-order Taylor expansion of log⁡p⁡(y∣xk)\log p(y\mid x^{k}) around μk\mu_{k} yields:

p⁡(xk∣xk+1,y)≈𝒩⁡(xk,μk+Σk​gk,Σk),gk=∇x​log​p​(y∣x)|x=μk.p(x^{k}\mid x^{k+1},y)\approx\mathcal{N}\!\bigl(x^{k};\;\mu_{k}+\Sigma_{k}g_{k},\;\Sigma_{k}\bigr),\qquad g_{k}=\nabla_{x}\log p(y\mid x)\big|_{x=\mu_{k}}.

Sampling from the guided distribution therefore reduces to shifting the denoising mean by Σk​gk\Sigma_{k}g_{k} at each step, with no modification to the model itself. In our framework, yy is instantiated as the target LLM agent πe\pi_{e}, and gkg_{k} becomes the log-likelihood gradient of πe\pi_{e} with respect to the current latent state, steering world-model rollouts toward trajectories compatible with the agent under evaluation.

4 Autoregressive Diffusion World Models

We develop an autoregressive diffusion world model for off-policy evaluation of LLM agents. The core insight is that a globally policy-guided trajectory law can be exactly factored into a sequence of single-step conditionals, each fusing local action consistency with global policy guidance. We realize these conditionals as a guided diffusion process in a structured latent space, where the evaluation LLM agent directly steers the denoising at every step (Figure 2).

4.1 From Trajectory Guidance to Single-Step Conditionals

In our agentic setting, the behavior policy πb\pi_{b} is unknown and generally intractable, as trajectories in 𝒟\mathcal{D} may originate from different LLM configurations, prompting strategies, or agent versions. A natural starting point is importance sampling, which corrects for the mismatch between pπbp_{\pi_{b}} and pπep_{\pi_{e}} via policy-likelihood ratios. Since the environment transition cancels between pπep_{\pi_{e}} and pπbp_{\pi_{b}}, the target trajectory law satisfies:

pπe​(τ)=pπb​(τ)⋅∏t=1Tπe​(at∣ht)πb​(at∣ht),\displaystyle p_{\pi_{e}}(\tau)=p_{\pi_{b}}(\tau)\cdot\prod_{t=1}^{T}\frac{\pi_{e}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})}{\pi_{b}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})}, (1)

so log⁡pπe​(τ)=log⁡pπb​(τ)+∑tlog⁡πe​(at∣ht)−∑tlog⁡πb​(at∣ht)\log p_{\pi_{e}}(\tau)=\log p_{\pi_{b}}(\tau)+\sum_{t}\log\pi_{e}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})-\sum_{t}\log\pi_{b}(a_{t}\mid h_{t}). Since πb\pi_{b} is unavailable, and dropping it acts as a form of behavior regularization [17] that anchors the distribution to the support of 𝒟\mathcal{D}, we learn a generative model pθ​(τ)p_{\theta}(\tau) of the logged trajectory distribution via maximum likelihood, and introduce α>0\alpha>0 to control the correction strength, yielding the policy-guided target law:

qα​(τ∣πe)∝pθ​(τ)​exp⁡(α​∑t=1Tlog⁡πe​(at∣ht)),α>0.q_{\alpha}(\tau\mid\pi_{e})\;\propto\;p_{\theta}(\tau)\,\exp\!\Big(\alpha\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\pi_{e}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\Big),\qquad\alpha>0. (2)

When pθ=pπbp_{\theta}=p_{\pi_{b}} and α=1\alpha=1, this recovers pπep_{\pi_{e}} exactly; the full derivation is in Appendix B.

The target law (2) is defined over full trajectories, but cannot be instantiated directly for a black-box πe\pi_{e}. Since πe\pi_{e} is a black-box LLM that must observe oto_{t} before producing ata_{t}, the trajectory-level tilt ∑tlog⁡πe​(at∣ht)\sum_{t}\log\pi_{e}(a_{t}\mid h_{t}) cannot be evaluated without first generating all observations in causal order. This forces an autoregressive decomposition: the world model and πe\pi_{e} must alternate step by step, generating observations and actions one at a time. The following proposition, proved in Appendix C, characterizes the exact single-step conditional induced by (2).

Proposition 1 (Autoregressive conditional law).

Let qαq_{\alpha} be the policy-guided trajectory law (2). Then for every (ht,at)(h_{t},a_{t}):

qα​(ot+1∣ht,at;πe)∝pθ​(ot+1∣ht,at)​𝒞α​(ot+1,ht,at,πe),q_{\alpha}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t};\pi_{e})\;\propto\;p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t})\,\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(o_{t+1};h_{t},a_{t},\pi_{e}), (3)

where the continuation factor is:

𝒞α(ot+1;ht,at,πe):=𝔼τt+1:T∼pθ(⋅∣ht,at,ot+1)[exp(α∑u=t+1Tlogπe(au∣hu))].\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(o_{t+1};h_{t},a_{t},\pi_{e})\;:=\;\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{t+1:T}\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t},a_{t},o_{t+1})}\!\left[\exp\!\Big(\alpha\sum_{u=t+1}^{T}\log\pi_{e}(a_{u}\mid h_{u})\Big)\right]. (4)

Two candidates for ot+1o_{t+1} may be equally supported by pθ​(ot+1∣ht,at)p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t}) yet lead to futures with very different compatibility with πe\pi_{e}; 𝒞α\mathcal{C}_{\alpha} is precisely the term that distinguishes them. A Bayesian decomposition of pθ​(ot+1∣ht,at)p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t}) further separates the prior dynamics from the influence of ata_{t}, giving the central result of our framework.

Theorem 1 (Fused single-step conditional).

Let qαq_{\alpha} be the policy-guided trajectory law (2). For every (ht,at)(h_{t},a_{t}) and any ω>0\omega>0, η≥0\eta\geq 0:

q~ω,η​(ot+1∣ht,at;πe)∝pθ​(ot+1∣ht)⏟prior⋅pθ​(at∣ot+1,ht)ω⏟action posterior⋅𝒞α​(ot+1,ht,at,πe)η⏟policy continuation,\widetilde{q}_{\omega,\eta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t};\pi_{e})\;\propto\;\underbrace{p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t})}_{\text{prior}}\;\cdot\;\underbrace{p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid o_{t+1},h_{t})^{\omega}}_{\text{action posterior}}\;\cdot\;\underbrace{\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(o_{t+1};h_{t},a_{t},\pi_{e})^{\eta}}_{\text{policy continuation}}, (5)

where ω=η=1\omega=\eta=1 recovers the exact conditional induced by qαq_{\alpha}.

Remark 1 (Limiting cases of ω\omega and η\eta).

The parameters ω\omega and η\eta interpolate between degenerate regimes that illuminate the role of each guidance term. Setting η=0\eta=0 removes the policy continuation factor entirely, reducing q~ω,0\widetilde{q}_{\omega,0} to an action-posterior-weighted prior that simulates the behavior distribution with no correction toward πe\pi_{e}. Setting ω=0\omega=0 suppresses the action posterior, causing the model to generate observations from the unconditional prior pθ​(ot+1∣ht)p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t}) irrespective of ata_{t} and breaking action-consistency. The canonical choice ω=η=1\omega=\eta=1 recovers the exact conditional induced by qαq_{\alpha}. In practice, ω\omega is controlled by the CFG scale λ\lambda via ω=1+λ\omega=1+\lambda, and η\eta is annealed over the reverse process; both are treated as hyperparameters rather than tuned per environment.

The three factors play distinct roles. The prior pθ​(ot+1∣ht)p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t}) anchors generated observations to the support of the offline data. The action posterior pθ​(at∣ot+1,ht)ωp_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid o_{t+1},h_{t})^{\omega} injects current-step action information without a separate classifier, recovered directly from classifier-free guidance as shown in Section 4.2. The continuation factor 𝒞α\mathcal{C}_{\alpha} re-weights candidate observations by their long-horizon compatibility with πe\pi_{e}, ensuring the world model generates observations that open up futures where πe\pi_{e} can act effectively. Crucially, since (5) is a single-step conditional, πe\pi_{e} never needs to produce actions before observations are generated, fully resolving the circular dependency that prevents existing diffusion OPE methods from operating autoregressively. The proof is given in Appendix D. Each factor corresponds to a distinct gradient term in the score function, which we now realize as a guided diffusion process in latent space.

Since (5) is a product of three factors, its log decomposes into a sum, and differentiating with respect to ot+1o_{t+1} yields an additive score:

∇ot+1​log​q~ω,η=∇log⁡pθ​(ot+1∣ht)⏟prior score+ω​∇log⁡pθ​(at∣ot+1,ht)⏟action-posterior score+η​∇log⁡𝒞α​(ot+1,ht,at,πe)⏟continuation score.\nabla_{o_{t+1}}\log\widetilde{q}_{\omega,\eta}\;=\;\underbrace{\nabla\log p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t})}_{\text{prior score}}\;+\;\omega\underbrace{\nabla\log p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid o_{t+1},h_{t})}_{\text{action-posterior score}}\;+\;\eta\underbrace{\nabla\log\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(o_{t+1};h_{t},a_{t},\pi_{e})}_{\text{continuation score}}. (6)

This additive structure is precisely what makes guided diffusion applicable: each term can be approximated and injected independently into the reverse process without retraining the world model. The prior score is given directly by the score network; the action-posterior score is recovered from the difference between action-conditioned and unconditional outputs via classifier-free guidance; and the continuation score requires differentiating through πe\pi_{e}’s log-likelihoods along future rollouts. We realize all three in a structured latent space, as detailed next.

4.2 Guided Diffusion World Model

The product structure of Theorem 1 maps directly onto guided diffusion: each factor contributes an additive term to the score, and sampling reduces to running a guided reverse process with πe\pi_{e} steering the denoising at every step. To instantiate this in practice, we first specify the latent space in which the diffusion operates and how πe\pi_{e} reads world-model states.

Latent state and policy interface.

Observations in LLM agent tasks are raw text, which cannot be directly denoised. We therefore operate in a structured latent space. An encoder EE maps each observation to a compact representation zt=E⁡(ot)∈ℝdz_{t}=E(o_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and a projector GψG_{\psi} produces soft tokens o~t=Gψ​(zt)∈ℝnsoft×dLLM\tilde{o}_{t}=G_{\psi}(z_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\mathrm{soft}}\times d_{\mathrm{LLM}}} that πe\pi_{e} can read in its own embedding space. The world model operates on the latent history ht=(z1,a1,…,zt)h_{t}=(z_{1},a_{1},\dots,z_{t}), while πe\pi_{e} conditions on htπ=(o~1,a1,…,o~t)h_{t}^{\pi}=(\tilde{o}_{1},a_{1},\dots,\tilde{o}_{t}). A pretrained semantic encoder is insufficient for this role: two observations that differ only in a negation may be nearby in semantic space yet lead to entirely different dynamics, corrupting all three guidance terms in (9) simultaneously. We therefore train EE end-to-end jointly with the world-model components on 𝒟\mathcal{D}, so that the representation is shaped by the dynamics of the environment rather than surface semantics. The projector GψG_{\psi} is then fitted to the evaluation LLM with a contrastive InfoNCE objective [30]:

ℒψ=−12​B∑i=1B[logesi​i/κ∑jesi​j/κ+logesi​i/κ∑jesj​i/κ]+βB∑i=1B∥G¯ψ(zi)−e¯i∥22,\mathcal{L}_{\psi}=-\frac{1}{2B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\left[\log\frac{e^{s_{ii}/\kappa}}{\sum_{j}e^{s_{ij}/\kappa}}+\log\frac{e^{s_{ii}/\kappa}}{\sum_{j}e^{s_{ji}/\kappa}}\right]+\frac{\beta}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\bigl\|\bar{G}_{\psi}(z_{i})-\bar{e}_{i}\bigr\|_{2}^{2}, (7)

where si​j=cossim⁡(G¯ψ​(zi),e¯j)s_{ij}=\mathrm{cossim}(\bar{G}_{\psi}(z_{i}),\bar{e}_{j}), G¯ψ​(zi)\bar{G}_{\psi}(z_{i}) is the token-mean of the projected soft tokens, e¯i\bar{e}_{i} is the token-mean of the ground-truth πe\pi_{e} input embeddings, κ\kappa is a temperature, and β=0.1\beta=0.1 balances discriminability against distributional alignment with πe\pi_{e}’s embedding space. Two auxiliary losses shape the representation: an inverse dynamics loss ℒIDM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IDM}} encouraging action-aware latents, and a behavior cloning loss ℒBC\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BC}} providing a stable retrieval target for GψG_{\psi}; full definitions are in Section F.7.

Guided score.

Following classifier-free guidance [14], we parameterize the world model as a score network sθ​(zt+1k,k,htz,at)s_{\theta}(z_{t+1}^{k},k;h_{t}^{z},a_{t}). A causal Transformer encodes the latent history htzh_{t}^{z} from the sequence of (zu,au)(z_{u},a_{u}) pairs with a subsequent-step mask, so the summary at step tt depends only on past latents and actions. The score network is an MLP that receives the noised latent zt+1kz_{t+1}^{k}, the diffusion step kk, this history summary, and the action embedding through FiLM conditioning (Section F.6). To realize the prior and action-posterior factors of Theorem 1 without a classifier, we train sθs_{\theta} under two regimes by randomly masking ata_{t} with probability pp during training:

ℒDSM​(θ)=𝔼⁡[‖sθ​(zt+1k,k,htz,a~t)−∇zk​log​pk​(zt+1k∣zt+1)‖2],a~t={∅w.p. ​p,atotherwise.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\Big[\big\|s_{\theta}(z_{t+1}^{k},k;h_{t}^{z},\tilde{a}_{t})-\nabla_{z^{k}}\log p_{k}(z_{t+1}^{k}\mid z_{t+1})\big\|^{2}\Big],\quad\tilde{a}_{t}=\begin{cases}\emptyset&\text{w.p. }p,\\ a_{t}&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (8)

By Bayes’ rule, the difference between the action-conditioned and unconditional outputs recovers the score of the implicit action posterior pϕ​(at∣zt+1k,htz)p_{\phi}(a_{t}\mid z_{t+1}^{k},h_{t}^{z}), so classifier-free guidance with scale λ\lambda directly realizes the first two terms of (5), with ω=1+λ\omega=1+\lambda.

For the continuation term, the score ∇zt+1​log​𝒞α\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log\mathcal{C}_{\alpha} requires an expectation over all future trajectories and is intractable. At each diffusion step kk, the score network provides a denoised estimate z^t+1\hat{z}_{t+1}; we roll the world model forward from this estimate and differentiate through πe\pi_{e}’s log-likelihoods along the resulting trajectory. The complete guided score is:

s⁡(zt+1k,k,htz,at,πe)\displaystyle s(z_{t+1}^{k},k;h_{t}^{z},a_{t},\pi_{e}) =∇zt+1k​log​pθ​(zt+1k∣htz)+ω​∇zt+1k​log​pϕ​(at∣zt+1k,htz)\displaystyle=\nabla_{z_{t+1}^{k}}\log p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}^{k}\mid h_{t}^{z})+\omega\,\nabla_{z_{t+1}^{k}}\log p_{\phi}(a_{t}\mid z_{t+1}^{k},h_{t}^{z})
+ηkα∇z^t+1∑u=t+1Tlogπe(a^u∣huπ),\displaystyle\quad+\;\eta_{k}\,\alpha\,\nabla_{\hat{z}_{t+1}}\sum_{u=t+1}^{T}\log\pi_{e}(\hat{a}_{u}\mid h_{u}^{\pi}), (9)

where ηk\eta_{k} is annealed so that continuation guidance strengthens as z^t+1\hat{z}_{t+1} becomes more reliable late in the reverse process. The complete derivation of (9) from Theorem 1 is given in Appendix E.

Value estimation.

Given the guided transition model, we estimate J⁡(πe)J(\pi_{e}) by Monte Carlo rollout. At each step, πe\pi_{e} samples an action at∼πe(⋅∣htπ)a_{t}\sim\pi_{e}(\cdot\mid h_{t}^{\pi}), the world model generates the next latent zt+1z_{t+1} via the reverse diffusion process with score (9), and the reward head predicts r^t=rρ​(zt+1,htz)\hat{r}_{t}=r_{\rho}(z_{t+1},h_{t}^{z}). Episodes terminate when the termination head d^t=σ⁡(dρ​(zt+1,htz))\hat{d}_{t}=\sigma(d_{\rho}(z_{t+1},h_{t}^{z})) exceeds a threshold. Averaging over MM rollouts gives:

J^​(πe)=1M​∑m=1M∑t=1Tmr^t(m),\displaystyle\widehat{J}(\pi_{e})=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{m}}\hat{r}_{t}^{(m)}, (10)

where TmT_{m} is the termination step of the mm-th rollout. The rollout follows the causal order of the real interaction: πe\pi_{e} reads only the soft tokens o~1:t\tilde{o}_{1:t} produced by the world model, and each next latent is generated only after ata_{t} is sampled. Hence no environment interaction is required at evaluation time.

5 Experiments

We evaluate Adwm around three questions:

  1. 1.

    Can a world model rank unseen policies from behavior data alone?

  2. 2.

    How does it compare to classical OPE under realistic LLM importance ratios?

  3. 3.

    Which components of the diffusion guidance matter?

Experiment setup.

We evaluate Adwm on four LLM-agent benchmarks chosen to span the reward and post-training regimes of modern LLM agents. On the reward axis, the suite covers dense per-step reward (HotpotQA F1 [39]), shaped partial reward (ScienceWorld [37]), continuous partial reward (WebShop [40]), and sparse binary success (ALFWorld [33]). On the policy axis, the cells cover task-specific RLHF-style post-training (DPO and PRM on HotpotQA [38]; ETO on ScienceWorld [34]) and generic-to-specialized iterative fine-tuning (LEAP on ALFWorld and WebShop [4]). All evaluation policies are publicly released checkpoints from prior work, summarised alongside their behavior counterparts in Table 1. Representative logged interaction traces for WebShop and ALFWorld are provided in Sections F.11 and F.12.

In every cell, the behavior policy πb\pi_{b} used to collect world-model training trajectories is strictly distinct from the evaluation policy πe\pi_{e} being scored. Concretely, πb\pi_{b} is either the matching task-specific SFT base of the same agent (HotpotQA, ScienceWorld) or, when no such base has been publicly released, the generic instruction-tuned Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [10] (ALFWorld, WebShop); the ALFWorld-iter3 and WebShop pools also include two other LEAP iterates (Table 3). The world model is therefore trained without ever observing πe\pi_{e}. On ALFWorld we additionally evaluate the third LEAP iteration to test cross-iteration ranking; on HotpotQA we pool DPO and PRM checkpoints into a 10-cell cross-policy split that probes policy-level discrimination beyond the within-policy ε\varepsilon-axis.

To assess sensitivity across a graded range of policy quality, we construct a one-parameter family of evaluation policies via ε\varepsilon-greedy mixing: at each step, πe\pi_{e} acts with probability 1−ε1{-}\varepsilon and a uniformly random admissible action is taken with probability ε\varepsilon, for ε∈{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0}\varepsilon\in\{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0\}. The real-environment ground-truth curve is obtained by executing πeε\pi_{e}^{\varepsilon} in the actual benchmark; Adwm produces J^\hat{J} entirely from world-model rollouts with no environment access at evaluation time. We run five random seeds per cell and report the Spearman rank correlation between the seed-averaged J^\hat{J} curve and the ground-truth curve. Full experimental details are in Appendix F.

The behavior and evaluation policies are not close. We measure the shift by the cumulative trajectory log-likelihood ratio:

log⁡pπe​(τ)pπb​(τ)=∑t=1Tlog⁡πe​(at∣ht)πb​(at∣ht).\log\frac{p_{\pi_{e}}(\tau)}{p_{\pi_{b}}(\tau)}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\frac{\pi_{e}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})}{\pi_{b}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})}.

At ε=0.5\varepsilon{=}0.5, its magnitude reaches up to 2424, 1818, 3535, and 2828 nats on HotpotQA, ScienceWorld, ALFWorld, and WebShop, so the trajectory likelihood ratios span roughly 1616 to 3030 orders of magnitude (Section G.3). The evaluation checkpoint is also excluded from every behavior pool. The experiments therefore go beyond the near-policy regime, although they do not cover fully out-of-support or cross-family evaluation.

Baselines.

We compare Adwm against five classical OPE estimators: direct method (DM) [36], importance sampling (IS) [32], weighted importance sampling (WIS) [32], fitted-Q evaluation (FQE) [24], and doubly robust estimation (DR) [20], all implemented following the COBS reference protocol [36]. For estimators that require πb\pi_{b} (IS, WIS, DR), we supply token log-probabilities of the logged actions under the behavior LLM rather than the uniform action prior commonly used in prior work, providing these baselines with privileged information that is unavailable in realistic deployments (closed-source APIs, deleted checkpoints, hidden tokenizers). We include them as diagnostic references rather than competitive baselines, since the unbounded LLM action space and limited distributional overlap in long-horizon rollouts violate the absolute-continuity assumption underlying IS-based estimators. Implementation details and the per-ε\varepsilon FQE correction are in Appendix G.

5.1 Results

Main results.

Table 2 compares Adwm against all five classical estimators across six (πb,πe)(\pi_{b},\pi_{e}) configurations. Adwm is the only estimator with strictly positive Spearman ρ\rho in every cell, ranging from +0.67+0.67 on ALFWorld-iter1 to +0.90+0.90 on both HotpotQA-DPO and WebShop-iter1 (mean +0.82+0.82), while every classical baseline is non-positive in at least two cells. IS and DR collapse under LLM-induced importance ratios spanning up to thirty orders of magnitude, with correlations as low as −0.90-0.90. WIS eliminates the explosion but degenerates to a single dominant-weight trajectory over long horizons, producing ρ=0\rho{=}0 on both ALFWorld cells and spurious positive correlations elsewhere driven by floating-point underflow ties. DM estimates a behavior-policy state value invariant to the evaluation policy’s action distribution, yielding ρ=0\rho{=}0 within every ε\varepsilon-sweep and inverting on the cross-policy split (ρ=−0.45\rho{=}{-}0.45). FQE is the sole partial exception: once corrected for the ε\varepsilon-linearity artifact in the COBS protocol, it attains ρ=+0.82\rho{=}{+}0.82 on ALFWorld-iter1 but collapses or inverts elsewhere (mean ρ=+0.10\rho{=}{+}0.10). Adwm, requiring neither importance weights nor a linear inductive bias, outperforms the next-best baseline by +0.34+0.34 in mean correlation; the world model is trained exclusively on πb\pi_{b} trajectories in every cell. Per-seed statistics and J^\hat{J}/GT curves are in Appendix H.

Training convergence.

Figure 3 shows that all loss components converge stably across all four benchmarks within 50 epochs. Beyond ℒDSM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}} (8), the total objective ℒWM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{WM}} includes two auxiliary terms: an inverse dynamics loss ℒIDM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IDM}} that predicts the bridging action between consecutive latents, encouraging action-aware representations, and a behavior cloning loss ℒBC\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BC}} that provides a stable retrieval target for the ψ\psi adapter. ℒDSM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DSM}} converges fastest; ℒIDM\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{IDM}} and ℒBC\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BC}} converge more gradually, consistent with the greater difficulty of predicting actions and cloning behavior on long-horizon text observations. Full definitions and loss weights are in Section F.7.

Ablations.

Figure 4 isolates the contribution of Adwm’s three core components across three environments with distinct reward structures. Each component dominates in a different reward regime, and no single component suffices across the full suite. Local CFG is most critical on long-horizon partial-reward tasks: removing it collapses WebShop ρ\rho from +0.90+0.90 to +0.10+0.10 and drops ScienceWorld from +1.00+1.00 to +0.60+0.60, with a smaller drop on HotpotQA (+0.90→+0.70+0.90\to+0.70). Continuation guidance is the primary mechanism for keeping trajectories on a successful path when per-step reward is absent, with removal degrading WebShop to +0.30+0.30 and ScienceWorld to +0.90+0.90. The ψ\psi adapter dominates on linguistically rich environments: its removal drops HotpotQA to +0.40+0.40 and degrades both ScienceWorld and WebShop to +0.60+0.60. Adwm’s robustness therefore requires the combination of all three components. Additional ablations on the latent dimension and on the design of the ψ\psi adapter loss are given in Appendix I.

6 Limitations

The policy-ranking experiments rely mainly on ε\varepsilon-greedy variants of a small number of publicly released base policies, because released agent checkpoints with different performance levels on the same benchmark remain scarce. Spearman ρ\rho measures ranking rather than the calibration of absolute values, and we do not ablate the size or the behavior-policy diversity of the offline data. Adwm removes the token-level error chain within each observation, but transition errors may still propagate across environment steps, and we do not provide an end-to-end error bound. Finally, the soft-token projector is fitted to each evaluation LLM, although neither the offline trajectories nor the transition model need to be recollected or retrained. A natural extension is a hybrid protocol that uses Adwm for offline ranking and spends a small online budget only on the highest-ranked or hardest-to-distinguish policies. Details are in Appendix A.

7 Conclusion

We presented Adwm, an offline evaluation framework that estimates LLM agent policy value purely from pre-collected trajectories. The key contribution is an exact decomposition of a policy-guided trajectory law into autoregressive single-step conditionals, each realized as a guided diffusion process in which the evaluation policy steers every denoising step without retraining or explicit importance weights. Empirically, Adwm is the only estimator with consistently positive rank correlations across all six (πb,πe)(\pi_{b},\pi_{e}) configurations, with ablations confirming that robustness requires the combination of all three guidance components.

Supplementary Materials

Appendix A Limitations

Adwm has two practical scope conditions. First, like all OPE estimators, it is bottlenecked by ground-truth quality: on WebShop the binomial standard error on GT success rate (up to 4.5%4.5\% with 128128 episodes) is comparable to the gap between adjacent LEAP iterates (33–19%19\%), so finer cross-iterate distinctions require substantially more GT episodes. Second, the ψ\psi adapter is tied to the evaluation LLM’s embedding space, so each new evaluation LLM requires a short adapter fit, while neither the offline trajectories nor the world model need to be recollected or retrained. Neither condition reflects a fundamental limitation of the underlying formulation.

Appendix B Relation to Classical Importance Sampling

We show that the policy-guided target law (2) is the natural generalization of importance sampling to the setting where the behavior policy πb\pi_{b} is unknown, and that it recovers the evaluation trajectory law exactly when pθ=pπbp_{\theta}=p_{\pi_{b}} and α=1\alpha=1.

Classical importance sampling identity.

For any two policies πb\pi_{b} and πe\pi_{e}, the induced trajectory laws satisfy:

pπe​(τ)\displaystyle p_{\pi_{e}}(\tau) =μ⁡(o1)​∏t=1Tπe​(at∣ht)​P​(ot+1∣ht,at)\displaystyle=\mu(o_{1})\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{e}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\,P(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t})
=μ⁡(o1)​∏t=1Tπb​(at∣ht)​P​(ot+1∣ht,at)⋅∏t=1Tπe​(at∣ht)πb​(at∣ht)\displaystyle=\mu(o_{1})\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{b}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\,P(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t})\cdot\prod_{t=1}^{T}\frac{\pi_{e}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})}{\pi_{b}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})}
=pπb​(τ)⋅∏t=1Tπe​(at∣ht)πb​(at∣ht),\displaystyle=p_{\pi_{b}}(\tau)\cdot\prod_{t=1}^{T}\frac{\pi_{e}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})}{\pi_{b}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})}, (11)

where μ⁡(o1)\mu(o_{1}) and P⁡(ot+1∣ht,at)P(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t}) denote the initial observation law and the observation kernel induced by μ\mu, PP, and ℰ\mathcal{E} after marginalizing the latent states, and the environment term P⁡(ot+1∣ht,at)P(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t}) cancels between numerator and denominator. Taking logarithms,

log⁡pπe​(τ)=log⁡pπb​(τ)+∑t=1Tlog⁡πe​(at∣ht)−∑t=1Tlog⁡πb​(at∣ht).\displaystyle\log p_{\pi_{e}}(\tau)=\log p_{\pi_{b}}(\tau)+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\pi_{e}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\pi_{b}(a_{t}\mid h_{t}). (12)

Equation (12) is the starting point shared by importance sampling, policy-guided diffusion [17], and STITCH-OPE [9]: the target trajectory law differs from the behavior trajectory law by a trajectory-level policy-likelihood correction.

Why πb\pi_{b} is unavailable.

In our agentic setting, the offline dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} may aggregate trajectories from heterogeneous sources—different prompting strategies, decoding configurations, or agent versions. The behavior policy πb\pi_{b} is therefore a mixture whose density πb​(at∣ht)\pi_{b}(a_{t}\mid h_{t}) is generally unavailable in closed form, preventing direct instantiation of (11).

From IS to the policy-guided target law.

We replace the unknown pπb​(τ)p_{\pi_{b}}(\tau) with a learned generative model pθ​(τ)p_{\theta}(\tau) trained on 𝒟\mathcal{D} by maximum likelihood. Dropping the negative behavior term −∑tlogπb(at∣ht)-\sum_{t}\log\pi_{b}(a_{t}\mid h_{t}) from (12) acts as a form of behavior regularization [17]: it anchors the target distribution to the support of the offline data rather than allowing unbounded correction away from it. Exponentiating and introducing a strength parameter α>0\alpha>0 yields:

qα​(τ∣πe)∝pθ​(τ)​exp⁡(α​∑t=1Tlog⁡πe​(at∣ht)),\displaystyle q_{\alpha}(\tau\mid\pi_{e})\;\propto\;p_{\theta}(\tau)\,\exp\!\Big(\alpha\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\pi_{e}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\Big), (13)

which is (2) in the main text.

Recovery of pπep_{\pi_{e}} at pθ=pπbp_{\theta}=p_{\pi_{b}}, α=1\alpha=1.

Suppose the learned prior is exact, i.e. pθ=pπbp_{\theta}=p_{\pi_{b}}. Then (13) with α=1\alpha=1 gives:

q1​(τ∣πe)\displaystyle q_{1}(\tau\mid\pi_{e}) ∝pπb​(τ)​exp⁡(∑t=1Tlog⁡πe​(at∣ht))\displaystyle\;\propto\;p_{\pi_{b}}(\tau)\,\exp\!\Big(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\pi_{e}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\Big)
=pπb​(τ)​∏t=1Tπe​(at∣ht).\displaystyle=p_{\pi_{b}}(\tau)\,\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{e}(a_{t}\mid h_{t}). (14)

The normalizing constant of (14) is:

Z\displaystyle Z =∫pπb​(τ)​∏t=1Tπe​(at∣ht)​𝑑τ\displaystyle=\int p_{\pi_{b}}(\tau)\,\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{e}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\,d\tau
=∫μ⁡(o1)​∏t=1Tπb​(at∣ht)​P​(ot+1∣ht,at)⋅∏t=1Tπe​(at∣ht)​𝑑τ.\displaystyle=\int\mu(o_{1})\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{b}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\,P(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t})\cdot\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{e}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\,d\tau. (15)

Using (11) to substitute pπb​(τ)​∏tπe​(at∣ht)/πb​(at∣ht)=pπe​(τ)p_{\pi_{b}}(\tau)\prod_{t}\pi_{e}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})/\pi_{b}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})=p_{\pi_{e}}(\tau):

Z\displaystyle Z =∫pπb​(τ)​∏t=1Tπe​(at∣ht)πb​(at∣ht)⋅∏t=1Tπb​(at∣ht)​𝑑τ\displaystyle=\int p_{\pi_{b}}(\tau)\,\prod_{t=1}^{T}\frac{\pi_{e}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})}{\pi_{b}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})}\cdot\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{b}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\,d\tau
=∫pπe​(τ)​𝑑τ= 1.\displaystyle=\int p_{\pi_{e}}(\tau)\,d\tau\;=\;1. (16)

Therefore (14) is already normalized, and:

q1​(τ∣πe)|pθ=pπb=pπb​(τ)​∏t=1Tπe​(at∣ht)=pπe​(τ),\displaystyle q_{1}(\tau\mid\pi_{e})\Big|_{p_{\theta}=p_{\pi_{b}}}\;=\;p_{\pi_{b}}(\tau)\,\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{e}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})\;=\;p_{\pi_{e}}(\tau), (17)

where the last equality follows from (11). This confirms that qαq_{\alpha} with α=1\alpha=1 and pθ=pπbp_{\theta}=p_{\pi_{b}} recovers the evaluation trajectory law exactly.

Role of α\alpha.

For α≠1\alpha\neq 1 or pθ≠pπbp_{\theta}\neq p_{\pi_{b}}, qα​(τ∣πe)q_{\alpha}(\tau\mid\pi_{e}) interpolates between the offline prior (α→0\alpha\to 0, recovering pθp_{\theta}) and a distribution that increasingly concentrates on trajectories preferred by πe\pi_{e} (α→∞\alpha\to\infty). In practice, α\alpha is a hyperparameter that balances the fidelity of the simulated environment against the alignment of generated rollouts with the evaluation policy.

Appendix C Proof of Proposition 1

We derive the single-step conditional law for ot+1o_{t+1} induced by the policy-guided trajectory law qα​(τ∣πe)q_{\alpha}(\tau\mid\pi_{e}) defined in (2).

Fix a history ht=(o1,a1,…,ot)h_{t}=(o_{1},a_{1},\dots,o_{t}) and a current action ata_{t}. We wish to characterize the conditional distribution qα​(ot+1∣ht,at;πe)q_{\alpha}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t};\pi_{e}). Denote the future suffix trajectory as:

τt+1:T=(ot+1,at+1,ot+2,…,aT,oT+1),\tau_{t+1:T}=(o_{t+1},a_{t+1},o_{t+2},\dots,a_{T},o_{T+1}),

so that the full trajectory decomposes as τ=(ht,at,τt+1:T)\tau=(h_{t},a_{t},\tau_{t+1:T}).

By definition of qαq_{\alpha} in (2), the unnormalized density of any trajectory τ\tau is:

qα​(τ∣πe)∝pθ​(τ)​exp⁡(α​∑t′=1Tlog⁡πe​(at′∣ht′)).q_{\alpha}(\tau\mid\pi_{e})\propto p_{\theta}(\tau)\,\exp\!\Bigl(\alpha\sum_{t^{\prime}=1}^{T}\log\pi_{e}(a_{t^{\prime}}\mid h_{t^{\prime}})\Bigr).

Conditioning on (ht,at)(h_{t},a_{t}) amounts to fixing all variables up to and including ata_{t}. The terms ∑t′=1tlog⁡πe​(at′∣ht′)\sum_{t^{\prime}=1}^{t}\log\pi_{e}(a_{t^{\prime}}\mid h_{t^{\prime}}) in the exponent are therefore constant with respect to the future suffix τt+1:T\tau_{t+1:T}, and are absorbed into the normalizing constant. We obtain:

qα(τt+1:T∣ht,at;πe)\displaystyle q_{\alpha}(\tau_{t+1:T}\mid h_{t},a_{t};\pi_{e}) =qα​(τ∣πe)qα​(ht,at∣πe)\displaystyle=\frac{q_{\alpha}(\tau\mid\pi_{e})}{q_{\alpha}(h_{t},a_{t}\mid\pi_{e})}
∝pθ(τt+1:T∣ht,at)exp(α∑u=t+1Tlogπe(au∣hu)),\displaystyle\propto p_{\theta}(\tau_{t+1:T}\mid h_{t},a_{t})\,\exp\!\Bigl(\alpha\sum_{u=t+1}^{T}\log\pi_{e}(a_{u}\mid h_{u})\Bigr), (18)

where we have used the fact that pθ(τ)=pθ(ht,at)⋅pθ(τt+1:T∣ht,at)p_{\theta}(\tau)=p_{\theta}(h_{t},a_{t})\cdot p_{\theta}(\tau_{t+1:T}\mid h_{t},a_{t}) by the chain rule of probability.

We now factor pθ(τt+1:T∣ht,at)p_{\theta}(\tau_{t+1:T}\mid h_{t},a_{t}) by separating out ot+1o_{t+1} from the remaining suffix. By the chain rule:

pθ(τt+1:T∣ht,at)=pθ(ot+1∣ht,at)pθ(τt+2:T∣ht,at,ot+1),\displaystyle p_{\theta}(\tau_{t+1:T}\mid h_{t},a_{t})=p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t})\,p_{\theta}(\tau_{t+2:T}\mid h_{t},a_{t},o_{t+1}), (19)

where we write τt+2:T=(at+1,ot+2,…,aT,oT+1)\tau_{t+2:T}=(a_{t+1},o_{t+2},\dots,a_{T},o_{T+1}) for the suffix starting after ot+1o_{t+1}. Note that once ot+1o_{t+1} is fixed, the updated history is ht+1=(ht,at,ot+1)h_{t+1}=(h_{t},a_{t},o_{t+1}), so pθ(τt+2:T∣ht,at,ot+1)=pθ(τt+2:T∣ht+1)p_{\theta}(\tau_{t+2:T}\mid h_{t},a_{t},o_{t+1})=p_{\theta}(\tau_{t+2:T}\mid h_{t+1}).

Substituting (19) into (18):

qα(τt+1:T∣ht,at;πe)∝pθ(ot+1∣ht,at)pθ(τt+2:T∣ht+1)exp(α∑u=t+1Tlogπe(au∣hu)).\displaystyle q_{\alpha}(\tau_{t+1:T}\mid h_{t},a_{t};\pi_{e})\propto p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t})\,p_{\theta}(\tau_{t+2:T}\mid h_{t+1})\,\exp\!\Bigl(\alpha\sum_{u=t+1}^{T}\log\pi_{e}(a_{u}\mid h_{u})\Bigr). (20)

To obtain the marginal over ot+1o_{t+1}, we integrate (20) over all remaining future variables τt+2:T\tau_{t+2:T}:

qα​(ot+1∣ht,at;πe)\displaystyle q_{\alpha}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t};\pi_{e}) =∫qα(τt+1:T∣ht,at;πe)dτt+2:T\displaystyle=\int q_{\alpha}(\tau_{t+1:T}\mid h_{t},a_{t};\pi_{e})\,d\tau_{t+2:T}
∝pθ(ot+1∣ht,at)∫pθ(τt+2:T∣ht+1)exp(α∑u=t+1Tlogπe(au∣hu))dτt+2:T.\displaystyle\propto p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t})\int p_{\theta}(\tau_{t+2:T}\mid h_{t+1})\,\exp\!\Bigl(\alpha\sum_{u=t+1}^{T}\log\pi_{e}(a_{u}\mid h_{u})\Bigr)\,d\tau_{t+2:T}. (21)

∫pθ(τt+2:T∣ht+1)exp(α∑u=t+1Tlogπe(au∣hu))dτt+2:T\displaystyle\int p_{\theta}(\tau_{t+2:T}\mid h_{t+1})\,\exp\!\Bigl(\alpha\sum_{u=t+1}^{T}\log\pi_{e}(a_{u}\mid h_{u})\Bigr)\,d\tau_{t+2:T}
