=𝔼τt+1:T∼pθ(⋅∣ht,at,ot+1)[exp(α∑u=t+1Tlogπe(au∣hu))],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{t+1:T}\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t},a_{t},o_{t+1})}\!\left[\exp\!\Bigl(\alpha\sum_{u=t+1}^{T}\log\pi_{e}(a_{u}\mid h_{u})\Bigr)\right], (22)

where in the second equality we have re-expressed the integral as an expectation over the full future suffix τt+1:T\tau_{t+1:T} conditioned on (ht,at,ot+1)(h_{t},a_{t},o_{t+1}), noting that integrating over τt+2:T\tau_{t+2:T} under pθ(⋅∣ht+1)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t+1}) is equivalent to integrating over τt+1:T\tau_{t+1:T} under pθ(⋅∣ht,at,ot+1)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t},a_{t},o_{t+1}) since the ot+1o_{t+1} component is fixed in both cases.

The expectation in (22) is precisely the continuation factor 𝒞α​(ot+1,ht,at,πe)\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(o_{t+1};h_{t},a_{t},\pi_{e}) defined in (4). Substituting back into (21):

qα​(ot+1∣ht,at;πe)∝pθ​(ot+1∣ht,at)​𝒞α​(ot+1,ht,at,πe).\displaystyle q_{\alpha}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t};\pi_{e})\propto p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t})\,\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(o_{t+1};h_{t},a_{t},\pi_{e}). (23)

This is precisely (3), completing the proof. □\square

Appendix D Proof of Theorem 1

We derive the fused single-step conditional law (5) from Proposition 1.

By Proposition 1, the single-step conditional induced by qαq_{\alpha} satisfies:

qα​(ot+1∣ht,at;πe)∝pθ​(ot+1∣ht,at)​𝒞α​(ot+1,ht,at,πe).q_{\alpha}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t};\pi_{e})\propto p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t})\,\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(o_{t+1};h_{t},a_{t},\pi_{e}). (24)

It remains to decompose pθ​(ot+1∣ht,at)p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t}). Consider the joint distribution pθ​(ot+1,at∣ht)p_{\theta}(o_{t+1},a_{t}\mid h_{t}). By the chain rule, this factors in two ways:

pθ​(ot+1,at∣ht)\displaystyle p_{\theta}(o_{t+1},a_{t}\mid h_{t}) =pθ​(ot+1∣ht,at)​pθ​(at∣ht),\displaystyle=p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t})\,p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid h_{t}), (25)
pθ​(ot+1,at∣ht)\displaystyle p_{\theta}(o_{t+1},a_{t}\mid h_{t}) =pθ​(at∣ot+1,ht)​pθ​(ot+1∣ht).\displaystyle=p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid o_{t+1},h_{t})\,p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t}). (26)

Equating (25) and (26):

pθ​(ot+1∣ht,at)​pθ​(at∣ht)=pθ​(at∣ot+1,ht)​pθ​(ot+1∣ht).p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t})\,p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})=p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid o_{t+1},h_{t})\,p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t}). (27)

Dividing both sides by pθ​(at∣ht)>0p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})>0:

pθ​(ot+1∣ht,at)=pθ​(at∣ot+1,ht)​pθ​(ot+1∣ht)pθ​(at∣ht).p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t})=\frac{p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid o_{t+1},h_{t})\,p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t})}{p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})}. (28)

Since pθ​(at∣ht)p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid h_{t}) is constant with respect to ot+1o_{t+1} for fixed (ht,at)(h_{t},a_{t}), (28) gives:

pθ​(ot+1∣ht,at)∝pθ​(ot+1∣ht)​pθ​(at∣ot+1,ht).p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t})\propto p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t})\,p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid o_{t+1},h_{t}). (29)

Substituting (29) into (24):

qα​(ot+1∣ht,at;πe)∝pθ​(ot+1∣ht)​pθ​(at∣ot+1,ht)​𝒞α​(ot+1,ht,at,πe),q_{\alpha}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t};\pi_{e})\propto p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t})\,p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid o_{t+1},h_{t})\,\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(o_{t+1};h_{t},a_{t},\pi_{e}), (30)

which is the ω=η=1\omega=\eta=1 case of (5).

For general ω>0\omega>0 and η≥0\eta\geq 0, we introduce the steered family by replacing each factor with its ω\omega-th and η\eta-th power respectively. This corresponds to treating ω\omega and η\eta as inverse temperatures on the action posterior and continuation factor, giving:

q~ω,η​(ot+1∣ht,at;πe)∝pθ​(ot+1∣ht)​pθ​(at∣ot+1,ht)ω​𝒞α​(ot+1,ht,at,πe)η.\widetilde{q}_{\omega,\eta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t};\pi_{e})\propto p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t})\,p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid o_{t+1},h_{t})^{\omega}\,\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(o_{t+1};h_{t},a_{t},\pi_{e})^{\eta}. (31)

This is (5), completing the proof. □\square

Remark 2.

The denominator pθ​(at∣ht)p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid h_{t}) in (28) depends only on (ht,at)(h_{t},a_{t}) and not on ot+1o_{t+1}. It is therefore a constant with respect to the variable of integration and is absorbed into the normalizing constant of the conditional distribution.

Remark 3.

The steered family q~ω,η\widetilde{q}_{\omega,\eta} is a valid probability distribution for any ω>0\omega>0 and η≥0\eta\geq 0, provided the normalizing constant

Z⁡(ω,η,ht,at)=∫pθ​(ot+1∣ht)​pθ​(at∣ot+1,ht)ω​𝒞α​(ot+1,ht,at,πe)η​d​ot+1Z(\omega,\eta;h_{t},a_{t})=\int p_{\theta}(o_{t+1}\mid h_{t})\,p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid o_{t+1},h_{t})^{\omega}\,\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(o_{t+1};h_{t},a_{t},\pi_{e})^{\eta}\,do_{t+1}

is finite, which holds under standard regularity conditions on pθp_{\theta} and πe\pi_{e}.

Appendix E Derivation of the Guided Score Function

We derive (9) in three steps, using the notation of Section 4.2: (i) decompose the score of the fused conditional into three additive terms; (ii) show that the first two terms are realized by classifier-free guidance; (iii) derive the tractable approximation of the continuation score.

E.1 Score decomposition of the fused conditional

By Theorem 1, the target single-step conditional is:

q~ω,η​(zt+1∣htz,at;πe)∝pθ​(zt+1∣htz)1⋅pϕ​(at∣zt+1,htz)ω⋅𝒞α​(zt+1,htz,at,πe)η.\displaystyle\widetilde{q}_{\omega,\eta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z},a_{t};\pi_{e})\;\propto\;p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z})^{1}\cdot p_{\phi}(a_{t}\mid z_{t+1},h_{t}^{z})^{\omega}\cdot\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(z_{t+1};h_{t}^{z},a_{t},\pi_{e})^{\eta}. (32)

Taking logarithms:

log⁡q~ω,η​(zt+1∣htz,at;πe)=log⁡pθ​(zt+1∣htz)+ω​log​pϕ​(at∣zt+1,htz)+η​log​𝒞α​(zt+1,htz,at,πe)+const,\displaystyle\log\widetilde{q}_{\omega,\eta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z},a_{t};\pi_{e})=\log p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z})+\omega\log p_{\phi}(a_{t}\mid z_{t+1},h_{t}^{z})+\eta\log\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(z_{t+1};h_{t}^{z},a_{t},\pi_{e})+\text{const}, (33)

where the constant absorbs the normalizer, which does not depend on zt+1z_{t+1}. Differentiating with respect to zt+1z_{t+1} gives the exact score:

∇zt+1​log​q~ω,η=∇zt+1​log​pθ​(zt+1∣htz)⏟prior score+ω​∇zt+1​log​pϕ​(at∣zt+1,htz)⏟action-posterior score+η​∇zt+1​log​𝒞α​(zt+1,htz,at,πe)⏟continuation score.\displaystyle\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log\widetilde{q}_{\omega,\eta}=\underbrace{\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z})}_{\text{prior score}}+\omega\underbrace{\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log p_{\phi}(a_{t}\mid z_{t+1},h_{t}^{z})}_{\text{action-posterior score}}+\eta\underbrace{\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(z_{t+1};h_{t}^{z},a_{t},\pi_{e})}_{\text{continuation score}}. (34)

Each term has a distinct role: the prior score keeps generated latents on the manifold of the offline data; the action-posterior score steers generation toward latents from which ata_{t} is recoverable; the continuation score steers generation toward latents that open up futures compatible with πe\pi_{e}.

E.2 Realization of the prior and action-posterior scores via classifier-free guidance

We show that the first two terms of (34) are jointly realized by classifier-free guidance [14] without a separate classifier.

Consider the joint density pθ​(zt+1,at∣htz)p_{\theta}(z_{t+1},a_{t}\mid h_{t}^{z}). By the chain rule it factors in two ways:

pθ​(zt+1,at∣htz)\displaystyle p_{\theta}(z_{t+1},a_{t}\mid h_{t}^{z}) =pθ​(zt+1∣htz,at)​pθ​(at∣htz),\displaystyle=p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z},a_{t})\,p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid h_{t}^{z}), (35)
pθ​(zt+1,at∣htz)\displaystyle p_{\theta}(z_{t+1},a_{t}\mid h_{t}^{z}) =pϕ​(at∣zt+1,htz)​pθ​(zt+1∣htz).\displaystyle=p_{\phi}(a_{t}\mid z_{t+1},h_{t}^{z})\,p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z}). (36)

Equating (35) and (36) and dividing both sides by pθ​(at∣htz)>0p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid h_{t}^{z})>0:

pθ​(zt+1∣htz,at)=pϕ​(at∣zt+1,htz)​pθ​(zt+1∣htz)pθ​(at∣htz).\displaystyle p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z},a_{t})=\frac{p_{\phi}(a_{t}\mid z_{t+1},h_{t}^{z})\,p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z})}{p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid h_{t}^{z})}. (37)

Taking logarithms and differentiating with respect to zt+1z_{t+1}, noting that pθ​(at∣htz)p_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid h_{t}^{z}) is constant in zt+1z_{t+1}:

∇zt+1​log​pθ​(zt+1∣htz,at)=∇zt+1​log​pθ​(zt+1∣htz)+∇zt+1​log​pϕ​(at∣zt+1,htz).\displaystyle\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z},a_{t})=\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z})+\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log p_{\phi}(a_{t}\mid z_{t+1},h_{t}^{z}). (38)

Rearranging:

∇zt+1​log​pϕ​(at∣zt+1,htz)=∇zt+1​log​pθ​(zt+1∣htz,at)−∇zt+1​log​pθ​(zt+1∣htz).\displaystyle\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log p_{\phi}(a_{t}\mid z_{t+1},h_{t}^{z})=\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z},a_{t})-\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z}). (39)

Substituting (39) into the first two terms of (34):

∇zt+1​log​pθ​(zt+1∣htz)+ω​∇zt+1​log​pϕ​(at∣zt+1,htz)\displaystyle\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z})+\omega\,\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log p_{\phi}(a_{t}\mid z_{t+1},h_{t}^{z})
=∇zt+1​log​pθ​(zt+1∣htz)+ω⁡(∇zt+1​log​pθ​(zt+1∣htz,at)−∇zt+1​log​pθ​(zt+1∣htz))\displaystyle=\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z})+\omega\Big(\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z},a_{t})-\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z})\Big)
=(1−ω)​∇zt+1​log⁡pθ​(zt+1∣htz)+ω​∇zt+1​log⁡pθ​(zt+1∣htz,at).\displaystyle=(1-\omega)\,\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z})+\omega\,\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z},a_{t}). (40)

Writing ω=1+λ\omega=1+\lambda, (40) becomes:

(1+λ)​∇zt+1​log⁡pθ​(zt+1∣htz,at)−λ​∇zt+1​log⁡pθ​(zt+1∣htz),\displaystyle(1+\lambda)\,\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z},a_{t})-\lambda\,\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}\mid h_{t}^{z}), (41)

which is exactly the classifier-free guidance combination with scale λ\lambda. In practice, both scores are approximated by the action-conditioned and unconditional branches of the shared score network sθs_{\theta}, trained jointly via (8) with action dropout.

E.3 Tractable approximation of the continuation score

The continuation factor is defined as:

𝒞α(zt+1;htz,at,πe):=𝔼τt+1:T∼pθ(⋅∣htz,at,zt+1)[exp(α∑u=t+1Tlogπe(au∣huπ))].\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(z_{t+1};h_{t}^{z},a_{t},\pi_{e}):=\mathbb{E}_{\tau_{t+1:T}\sim p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{t}^{z},a_{t},z_{t+1})}\!\left[\exp\!\Big(\alpha\sum_{u=t+1}^{T}\log\pi_{e}(a_{u}\mid h_{u}^{\pi})\Big)\right]. (42)

Computing ∇zt+1​log​𝒞α\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log\mathcal{C}_{\alpha} exactly requires differentiating through an expectation over all future trajectories, which is intractable. We derive a tractable approximation via the denoised estimate.

At diffusion step kk, the score network provides the posterior mean estimate:

z^t+1=𝔼⁡[zt+1∣zt+1k]=zt+1k+(1−α¯k)​sθ​(zt+1k,k,htz,at)α¯k.\displaystyle\hat{z}_{t+1}=\mathbb{E}[z_{t+1}\mid z_{t+1}^{k}]=\frac{z_{t+1}^{k}+(1-\bar{\alpha}_{k})\,s_{\theta}(z_{t+1}^{k},k;h_{t}^{z},a_{t})}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{k}}}. (43)

We substitute z^t+1\hat{z}_{t+1} for zt+1z_{t+1} in (42) and replace the expectation over future trajectories with a single greedy rollout τ^t+1:T=ℛθ(z^t+1;htz,at)\hat{\tau}_{t+1:T}=\mathcal{R}_{\theta}(\hat{z}_{t+1};h_{t}^{z},a_{t}):

log⁡𝒞α​(zt+1,htz,at,πe)≈α​∑u=t+1Tlog⁡πe​(a^u∣huπ).\displaystyle\log\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}(z_{t+1};h_{t}^{z},a_{t},\pi_{e})\;\approx\;\alpha\sum_{u=t+1}^{T}\log\pi_{e}(\hat{a}_{u}\mid h_{u}^{\pi}). (44)

Differentiating (44) with respect to z^t+1\hat{z}_{t+1}, and using this gradient in place of the gradient with respect to zt+1kz_{t+1}^{k} (that is, dropping the Jacobian of (43)), gives the tractable continuation gradient:

η​∇zt+1​log⁡𝒞α≈ηk​α​∇z^t+1​∑u=t+1Tlog⁡πe​(a^u∣huπ),\displaystyle\eta\,\nabla_{z_{t+1}}\log\mathcal{C}_{\alpha}\;\approx\;\eta_{k}\,\alpha\,\nabla_{\hat{z}_{t+1}}\sum_{u=t+1}^{T}\log\pi_{e}(\hat{a}_{u}\mid h_{u}^{\pi}), (45)

where we write ηk\eta_{k} to allow the continuation weight to vary with noise level kk, suppressing the signal when z^t+1\hat{z}_{t+1} is unreliable at high noise and amplifying it late in the reverse process.

E.4 Final guided score

Combining (41) and (45), the complete guided score at noise level kk is:

s⁡(zt+1k,k,htz,at,πe)\displaystyle s(z_{t+1}^{k},k;h_{t}^{z},a_{t},\pi_{e}) =∇zt+1k​log​pθ​(zt+1k∣htz)+ω​∇zt+1k​log​pϕ​(at∣zt+1k,htz)\displaystyle=\nabla_{z_{t+1}^{k}}\log p_{\theta}(z_{t+1}^{k}\mid h_{t}^{z})+\omega\,\nabla_{z_{t+1}^{k}}\log p_{\phi}(a_{t}\mid z_{t+1}^{k},h_{t}^{z})
+ηkα∇z^t+1∑u=t+1Tlogπe(a^u∣huπ),\displaystyle\quad+\;\eta_{k}\,\alpha\,\nabla_{\hat{z}_{t+1}}\sum_{u=t+1}^{T}\log\pi_{e}(\hat{a}_{u}\mid h_{u}^{\pi}), (46)

which is (9) in the main text.

Appendix F Experimental Setup Details

F.1 Software stack and reproducibility

All training and OPE rollout code is implemented in PyTorch 2.6 with Transformers 4.56 under Python 3.10. LLM-side πb\pi_{b}/πe\pi_{e} inference is served by vLLM 0.8.5 with bf16 weights and a tensor-parallel size of 1 (one GPU per LLM job). Baselines (FQE, DR, IS, WIS, DM) are implemented to match the COBS reference protocol of Voloshin et al. [36] verbatim except for the per-ε\varepsilon FQE correction described in Section G.4. Random seeds s∈{0,1,2,3,4}s\in\{0,1,2,3,4\} control (i) the ε\varepsilon-greedy admissible-action draw and (ii) the imagined-rollout DDPM noise sequence. The world model and the ψ\psi adapter are trained once per behavior pool with a fixed seed; the five per-cell seeds vary inference-time stochasticity only.

F.2 Hardware and compute budget

All experiments run on a shared cluster node with 2×2\times Intel Xeon Gold 6248R (3.00 GHz, 96 logical cores) and 2×2\times NVIDIA Quadro RTX 8000 (48 GB) GPUs interconnected by PCIe 3.0 x16. We allocate a single GPU per training or evaluation job; multi-GPU parallelism is not used.

Wall-clock budget.

  • •

    World-model training (per environment): 50 epochs on 256–744 trajectories at batch size 64 takes 30–90 min.

  • •

    ψ\psi-adapter training (per environment): 20 epochs at batch size 8 takes 10–20 min.

  • •

    GT collection (per cell, per ε\varepsilon): vLLM-served πeε\pi_{e}^{\varepsilon} rolling out for 64–128 episodes takes 10–40 min depending on env horizon.

  • •

    Adwm inference (per cell, per seed): 5 ε\varepsilon levels ×\times 32 imagined rollouts ×\times horizon ≤30\leq 30 takes 15–45 min.

  • •

    FQE / DR (per cell, per seed): 5 ε\varepsilon-conditioned Q-nets at 20 epochs each takes 5–10 min.

Total cost.

The full camera-ready experimental suite (six (πb,πe)(\pi_{b},\pi_{e}) cells ×\times 5 seeds, plus 7 ablation variants on three environments, plus 5 baseline estimators per cell) consumes approximately 300300 GPU-hours, of which ∼\sim70%70\% is LLM-side (πb\pi_{b} and πe\pi_{e}) inference and ∼\sim25%25\% is GT collection. World-model training itself accounts for <5%<5\% of the budget — the dominant cost of Adwm is the same as the dominant cost of any LLM-agent OPE method, namely running the eval LLM.

F.3 Behavior-policy data

For each (πb,πe)(\pi_{b},\pi_{e}) cell we collect a single offline behavior pool that is reused across all ε\varepsilon levels and seeds for that cell. The world model is trained only on this pool. Table 3 summarises the per-cell trajectory counts, behavior models actually used, and observed empirical statistics. The HotpotQA, ScienceWorld, and ALFWorld-iter1 cells use a single behavior LLM each. The ALFWorld-iter3 and WebShop-iter1 cells use a three-LLM behavior pool consisting of the generic Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct together with two LEAP iterates (iter0\text{iter}_{0} and iter2\text{iter}_{2}); we exclude iter1\text{iter}_{1} from the WS pool and iter3\text{iter}_{3} from the ALF pool to ensure the eval policy is never in the behavior pool. This pooling choice mirrors a realistic deployment in which multiple released checkpoints from the same LEAP self-improvement chain may already be available offline. We verify post-hoc that no training trajectory in the pool was generated by the exact πe\pi_{e} checkpoint scored at evaluation time.

Trajectories are collected with greedy LLM decoding (temperature 0) and two system-prompt variants {p0,p1}\{p_{0},p_{1}\} that differ only in instruction phrasing (not task content), to obtain useful behavior coverage without changing the underlying πb\pi_{b}. Episode length is capped at 30 environment steps for ALFWorld and WebShop and at 12 for HotpotQA and ScienceWorld. Each recorded trajectory contains, per step,

(obs_textt,llm_responset,ut,at,avalidt,rt,donet),(\text{obs\_text}_{t},\text{llm\_response}_{t},u_{t},a_{t},a_{\text{valid}}^{t},r_{t},\text{done}_{t}),

where utu_{t} is the raw action text parsed from the LLM response and ata_{t} is the action actually passed to the environment after the environment-specific projection interface. We write this interface as

at∼Γenv(⋅∣ht,ut,𝒜adm(ht)).a_{t}\sim\Gamma_{\mathrm{env}}\!\left(\cdot\mid h_{t},u_{t},\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{adm}}(h_{t})\right).

The world-model transition tuples use the executed action ata_{t}, so (ot+1,rt)(o_{t+1},r_{t}) is paired with the action that generated it. The raw response and utu_{t} are retained as auxiliary logged text. Successful trajectories are upsampled 5×5\times during world-model training to counter class imbalance on the long-tail success distributions of Table 3.

F.4 Ground-truth episode counts

Per-cell ground-truth success curves are obtained by running πeε\pi_{e}^{\varepsilon} in the actual environment for nGTn_{\text{GT}} independent episodes per ε\varepsilon level, with seed 42 fixed across ε\varepsilon within a policy:

Cell nGTn_{\text{GT}} per ε\varepsilon
HotpotQA-DPO 128
HotpotQA-PRM 064
ScienceWorld-ETO 064
ALFWorld-iter1 / iter3 072
WebShop-iter1 128

The binomial standard error on the GT success rate at n=64n{=}64 is ≤6.3%\leq 6.3\% for any p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1), and ≤4.5%\leq 4.5\% at n=128n{=}128.

F.5 ε\varepsilon-greedy mixing protocol

Let π~e​(u∣h)\widetilde{\pi}_{e}(u\mid h) denote the evaluation LLM’s distribution over raw action text and let Γenv​(a∣h,u,𝒜adm​(h))\Gamma_{\mathrm{env}}(a\mid h,u,\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{adm}}(h)) denote the environment-specific projection from raw text to an executed admissible action. The induced executed-action policy is

πe,Γ​(a∣h)=∑uπ~e​(u∣h)​Γenv​(a∣h,u,𝒜adm​(h)).\pi_{e,\Gamma}(a\mid h)=\sum_{u}\widetilde{\pi}_{e}(u\mid h)\,\Gamma_{\mathrm{env}}\!\left(a\mid h,u,\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{adm}}(h)\right). (47)

This notation also covers a deterministic projection, in which Γenv\Gamma_{\mathrm{env}} is a point mass.

We apply ε\varepsilon-mixing to the executed-action policy:

πeε​(a∣h)=(1−ε)​πe,Γ​(a∣h)+ε​𝕀[a∈𝒜adm(h)]|𝒜adm​(h)|.\pi_{e}^{\varepsilon}(a\mid h)=(1-\varepsilon)\pi_{e,\Gamma}(a\mid h)+\varepsilon\frac{\mathbb{I}[a\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{adm}}(h)]}{|\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{adm}}(h)|}. (48)

Operationally, we sample one Bernoulli variable per step. With probability 1−ε1-\varepsilon, the LLM produces ut∼π~e(⋅∣ht)u_{t}\sim\widetilde{\pi}_{e}(\cdot\mid h_{t}) and the interface samples at∼Γenv(⋅∣ht,ut,𝒜adm(ht))a_{t}\sim\Gamma_{\mathrm{env}}(\cdot\mid h_{t},u_{t},\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{adm}}(h_{t})). With probability ε\varepsilon, we sample ata_{t} uniformly from the current admissible set. Both Adwm imagined rollouts and ground-truth environment rollouts use this same interface and random seed.

F.6 World-model architecture

The world model is a 7.4M-parameter latent diffusion model with the modular structure shown in Table 4. In this appendix we write fθf_{\theta}, h¯t\bar{h}_{t}, ϵθ\epsilon_{\theta}, RθR_{\theta}, and DθD_{\theta} for the encoder EE, the history summary of htzh_{t}^{z}, the noise-prediction form of the score network sθs_{\theta}, the reward head rρr_{\rho}, and the termination head dρd_{\rho} of Section 4.2. The largest component is the text-based observation encoder (5.05 M params), which tokenises raw obs_textt\text{obs\_text}_{t} via a stable hash-bucket tokeniser (vocabulary size 32,768, max length 128 tokens) and embeds it into the latent dimension dz=64d_{z}{=}64 through a 4-layer TransformerEncoder of width 128 with 4 attention heads. The history encoder is a causal 4-layer Transformer with width 128 and a generated subsequent-token mask, conditioning on (zt,at)(z_{t},a_{t}) tuples. The score network is a 3-layer FiLM-MLP of width 256 with sinusoidal time embedding (dimension 64) and zero-initialised output projection; the IDM and BC heads are 2-layer MLPs over (z,h)(z,h). All non-linearities are SiLU except the IDM / policy / projector heads, which use ReLU and GELU respectively.

The action vocabulary |𝒜||\mathcal{A}| is set per environment from the unique projected actions ata_{t} actually executed in the behavior pool, capped at 256; HotpotQA uses a fixed 4-action vocabulary {⟨unk⟩,search,lookup,finish}\{\langle\text{unk}\rangle,\,\text{search},\,\text{lookup},\,\text{finish}\} that matches the ReAct protocol of Yao et al. [41].

F.7 World-model training objective

The world model is trained with the multi-task objective

ℒWM=ℒDSM+λidm​ℒIDM+λbc​ℒBC+λdiv​ℒdiv+λr​ℒr+λd​ℒd,\mathcal{L}_{\text{WM}}\;=\;\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}}+\lambda_{\text{idm}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{IDM}}+\lambda_{\text{bc}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{BC}}+\lambda_{\text{div}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{div}}+\lambda_{\text{r}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{r}}+\lambda_{\text{d}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{d}}, (49)

with weights (λidm,λbc,λdiv,λr,λd)=(0.1, 0.1, 0.05, 10, 1)(\lambda_{\text{idm}},\lambda_{\text{bc}},\lambda_{\text{div}},\lambda_{\text{r}},\lambda_{\text{d}})=(0.1,\,0.1,\,0.05,\,10,\,1). The component losses are defined as follows.

(a) Denoising score matching (ℒDSM\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}}).

For a sampled diffusion step k∼Unif⁡(1,K)k\!\sim\!\mathrm{Unif}(1,K), latent z∼fθ​(obst+1)z\!\sim\!f_{\theta}(\text{obs}_{t+1}), history h¯t\bar{h}_{t}, and action ata_{t}, we form the noised latent zk=α¯k​z+1−α¯k​ξz_{k}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{k}}\,z+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{k}}\,\xi with ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\xi\!\sim\!\mathcal{N}(0,I) and a cosine α¯k\bar{\alpha}_{k} schedule. We train the conditional score network ϵθ​(zk,k,h¯t,at)\epsilon_{\theta}(z_{k},k,\bar{h}_{t},a_{t}) together with its unconditional counterpart ϵθ​(zk,k,h¯t,∅)\epsilon_{\theta}(z_{k},k,\bar{h}_{t},\varnothing) under classifier-free dropout puncond=0.1p_{\text{uncond}}{=}0.1:

ℒDSM=𝔼k,ξ​[w⁡(k)​(‖ϵθ​(zk,k,h¯t,at)−ξ‖22+‖ϵθ​(zk,k,h¯t,∅)−ξ‖22)],w⁡(k)= 1−α¯k.\mathcal{L}_{\text{DSM}}\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{k,\xi}\big[w(k)\,\big(\|\epsilon_{\theta}(z_{k},k,\bar{h}_{t},a_{t})-\xi\|_{2}^{2}+\|\epsilon_{\theta}(z_{k},k,\bar{h}_{t},\varnothing)-\xi\|_{2}^{2}\big)\big],\quad w(k)\,=\,1-\bar{\alpha}_{k}. (50)

The w⁡(k)=1−α¯kw(k)\!=\!1-\bar{\alpha}_{k} weighting keeps the per-step loss numerically comparable across kk. This is the noise-prediction form of (8), with sθ=−ϵθ/1−α¯ks_{\theta}=-\epsilon_{\theta}/\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{k}}.

(b) Inverse-dynamics regulariser (ℒIDM\mathcal{L}_{\text{IDM}}).

A discriminative auxiliary that predicts the bridging action between two consecutive latents: ℒIDM=CE⁡(IDM⁡(zt+1,h¯t),at)\mathcal{L}_{\text{IDM}}=\mathrm{CE}\big(\mathrm{IDM}(z_{t+1},\bar{h}_{t}),\,a_{t}\big). This pushes zz to be action-aware and prevents the diffusion prior from collapsing onto policy-invariant features.

(c) Behavior-cloning soft-token loss (ℒBC\mathcal{L}_{\text{BC}}).

ℒBC=CE⁡(BC⁡(zt,h¯t),at)\mathcal{L}_{\text{BC}}=\mathrm{CE}\big(\mathrm{BC}(z_{t},\bar{h}_{t}),\,a_{t}\big). Trains the latent-to-policy interface against logged actions independently of any specific evaluation policy, providing the ψ\psi-adapter retrieval target a stable signal.

(d) Diversity regulariser (ℒdiv\mathcal{L}_{\text{div}}).

A cross-trajectory contrastive penalty that prevents the latent space from collapsing across distinct trajectories. For batch {z1:L(i)}i=1B\{z^{(i)}_{1:L}\}_{i=1}^{B}, let z¯(i)=normalize⁡(meant​zt(i))\bar{z}^{(i)}=\mathrm{normalize}(\mathrm{mean}_{t}z^{(i)}_{t}) be the per-trajectory pooled latent. Then

ℒdiv=1B⁡(B−1)​∑i≠j|z¯(i)⊤​z¯(j)|.\mathcal{L}_{\text{div}}\;=\;\frac{1}{B(B-1)}\sum_{i\neq j}\big|\bar{z}^{(i)\,\top}\bar{z}^{(j)}\big|. (51)

Same-window adjacent latents are deliberately left free since the dynamics constraint requires them to stay close.

(e) Reward head (ℒr\mathcal{L}_{\text{r}}).

For environments with continuous reward (HotpotQA F1, ScienceWorld shaped reward, WebShop product match) we use MSE on sigmoid-clipped reward-to-go targets: ℒr=𝔼t​[(σ⁡(Rθ​(zt+1,h¯t))−rttgt)2]\mathcal{L}_{\text{r}}=\mathbb{E}_{t}\big[(\sigma(R_{\theta}(z_{t+1},\bar{h}_{t}))-r_{t}^{\text{tgt}})^{2}\big] with rttgt∈[0,1]r_{t}^{\text{tgt}}\in[0,1]. For sparse-reward ALFWorld we replace the MSE by a balanced binary cross-entropy with sigmoid output and per-batch positive-class weight min⁡(50,nneg/npos)\min(50,n_{\text{neg}}/n_{\text{pos}}), which prevents the reward head from collapsing to the constant p≈r¯p\!\approx\!\bar{r} predictor. The reward head is supervised on terminal steps only when the environment provides a terminal-only success label, and on all steps when shaped per-step rewards are available.

(f) Termination head (ℒd\mathcal{L}_{\text{d}}).

A binary cross-entropy with class-balanced positive weight min⁡(50,nneg/npos)\min(50,n_{\text{neg}}/n_{\text{pos}}): ℒd=BCE⁡(Dθ​(zt+1,h¯t), 1​[done at ​t+1])\mathcal{L}_{\text{d}}=\mathrm{BCE}\big(D_{\theta}(z_{t+1},\bar{h}_{t}),\,\mathbf{1}[\text{done at }t+1]\big). Used during imagined rollouts to terminate trajectories that the world model predicts have ended.

F.8 World-model training procedure

Algorithm 1 summarises the optimization . Each forward pass sampling a window of length LL within a trajectory builds a rolling-window prediction target: given (z1:L,a1:L−1)(z_{1:L},a_{1:L-1}), the model is trained to score the noisy version of every zt+1z_{t+1} conditional on h¯t\bar{h}_{t} and ata_{t}. The optimiser is AdamW with (β1,β2)=(0.9,0.999)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.999), weight decay 10−410^{-4}, peak learning rate ×10−43\!\times\!10^{-4}, cosine annealing to 10%10\% of peak over 50 epochs, batch size 64, gradient norm clip 1.0. WebShop and ALFWorld train under PyTorch automatic mixed precision (bf16 master + fp32 accumulator); HotpotQA and ScienceWorld train in fp32 because the smaller dataset fits comfortably in 48 GB.

F.9 ψ\psi-adapter training

The ψ\psi adapter projects latent observations into a sequence of soft tokens that drop into the input embedding space of πe\pi_{e}. This step is necessary because Eq. 9’s continuation guidance backpropagates a gradient through πe\pi_{e}’s frozen input layer; without an adapter that targets πe\pi_{e}’s embedding manifold, the gradient is meaningless. The adapter Gψ:ℝdz→ℝnsoft×dllmG_{\psi}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}}\to\mathbb{R}^{n_{\text{soft}}\times d_{\text{llm}}} is a 3-layer GELU MLP (dz→→→⋅dllmd_{z}\!\to\!256\!\to\!256\!\to\!8\!\cdot\!d_{\text{llm}}) with nsoft=8n_{\text{soft}}=8 soft tokens.

The training objective is a symmetric InfoNCE term plus a ×0.1\!\times MSE regulariser:

ℒψ=−12​B∑i=1B(logesi​i/κ∑jesi​j/κ+logesi​i/κ∑jesj​i/κ)⏟ℒInfoNCE+⋅1B​∑i=1B‖G¯ψ​(zi)−e¯i‖22⏟ℒMSE,\mathcal{L}_{\psi}\;=\;\underbrace{-\frac{1}{2B}\!\sum_{i=1}^{B}\!\Big(\!\log\!\frac{e^{s_{ii}/\kappa}}{\sum_{j}e^{s_{ij}/\kappa}}+\log\!\frac{e^{s_{ii}/\kappa}}{\sum_{j}e^{s_{ji}/\kappa}}\!\Big)}_{\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}}}\;+\;0.1\!\cdot\!\underbrace{\frac{1}{B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\big\|\bar{G}_{\psi}(z_{i})-\bar{e}_{i}\big\|_{2}^{2}}_{\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}}}, (52)

where si​j=cossim⁡(G¯ψ​(zi),e¯j)s_{ij}=\mathrm{cossim}(\bar{G}_{\psi}(z_{i}),\bar{e}_{j}), G¯ψ​(zi)=meann​Gψ​(zi)n\bar{G}_{\psi}(z_{i})=\mathrm{mean}_{n}G_{\psi}(z_{i})_{n} is the soft-token-mean of the projector, e¯j\bar{e}_{j} is the LLM-token-mean of the ground-truth πe\pi_{e} input embedding sequence, and κ=0.1\kappa{=}0.1. Pure MSE (ℒInfoNCE→0\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}}\!\to\!0) collapses because e¯j\bar{e}_{j} has low variance across observations, yielding ∂Gψ/∂z→0\partial G_{\psi}/\partial z\!\to\!0 and a vacuous Eq. 9 gradient; pure InfoNCE produces a discriminative adapter whose absolute outputs drift out-of-distribution for the LLM. The combined loss balances both. We optimise with Adam (lr=10−4\text{lr}{=}10^{-4}), batch size 8, for 20 epochs.

Final-epoch top-1 retrieval accuracy on the InfoNCE batch (random baseline 1/B=0.1251/B=0.125):

Cell ψ\psi top-1
HotpotQA 0.7150.715
ScienceWorld 0.3940.394
ALFWorld-iter1 0.5580.558
ALFWorld-iter3 0.4700.470
WebShop ∼0.10\sim 0.10

The WebShop adapter sits at the random-baseline floor: token-mean target embeddings of long product descriptions are nearly degenerate under cosine similarity, so the InfoNCE objective alone cannot discriminate them at batch size 8. Despite this, the adapter still provides a useful Eq. 9 gradient (rather than a useful retrieval) on WebShop, which is why ablating it still degrades ρ\rho by 0.30 (Fig. 4).

F.10 OPE-rollout protocol

Algorithm 2 summarises the imagined-rollout procedure used to compute J^\hat{J} at evaluation time. Each rollout is initialised from a uniformly sampled real-environment obs0\text{obs}_{0} in the behavior pool and encoded into z0∼fθ​(obs0)z_{0}\sim f_{\theta}(\text{obs}_{0}). At each step, the evaluation LLM first produces raw action text utu_{t} from the soft-token state Gψ​(zt)G_{\psi}(z_{t}). The same environment-specific projection used during data collection then maps utu_{t} to the executed action ata_{t}, with the ε\varepsilon-random branch applied as in Eq. 48. The diffusion world model samples zt+1z_{t+1} conditioned on this executed action ata_{t}, using both Eq. 8 (local CFG) and Eq. 9 (continuation guidance) at each denoising step. We use nroll=32n_{\text{roll}}{=}32 rollouts per cell (nroll=64n_{\text{roll}}{=}64 on ALFWorld-iter1 to compensate for binary-success Monte Carlo noise), maximum horizon Hmax=30H_{\max}{=}30 steps, ndenoise=50n_{\text{denoise}}{=}50 DDPM denoising steps per environment step, λCFG=1.0\lambda_{\text{CFG}}{=}1.0, and continuation-guidance hyperparameters (α=1.0,ηmax=0.5,h=5)(\alpha{=}1.0,\,\eta_{\max}{=}0.5,\,h{=}5). Rollouts terminate early when the termination head Dθ​(zt,h¯t)D_{\theta}(z_{t},\bar{h}_{t}) predicts Pr⁡[done]≥0.5\Pr[\text{done}]\!\geq\!0.5. Empirical mean rollout lengths after early termination: HP 8, SW/WS/ALF-iter3 12, ALF-iter1 18.

F.11 Example interaction trace: WebShop

To make the interaction notation in Section 3.1 concrete, we present two representative logged WebShop episodes from the 640-trajectory behavior pool used for the WebShop-iter1 cell in Table 3, comprising Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and leap-ws-iter{0,2} trajectories. Direct inspection of the pool gives N=640N=640, mean horizon 14.4214.42, and behavior-policy success rate 5.0%5.0\%, matching Table 3. Both examples below were generated by the Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct component, with episode identifiers 18 and 17. Thus, the logging policy and data source are consistent with the pool used to train the WebShop world model.

A logged episode has the form

τ=(o1,a1,r1,…,oT,aT,rT,oT+1).\tau=(o_{1},a_{1},r_{1},\ldots,o_{T},a_{T},r_{T},o_{T+1}).

At step tt, the policy conditions on the full interaction history

ht=(o1,a1,…,ot−1,at−1,ot)h_{t}=(o_{1},a_{1},\ldots,o_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_{t})

and produces a text action ata_{t}, stored as a reasoning response followed by an <action>...</action> tag. WebShop then returns the next observation ot+1o_{t+1}, reward rt∈[0,1]r_{t}\in[0,1], and a termination indicator. For Episode 1, we report the complete action–reward sequence and expand three representative reasoning steps. Episode 2 is shown as a concise trace focused on the graded terminal reward.

Episode Steps TT Terminal rTr_{T} Main phenomenon
1: makeup palette 16 1.01.0 The purchase succeeds despite the policy’s reasoning stating that the product does not match.
2: men’s shirt 5 0.7270.727 The selected listing does not offer the requested color or size, but receives graded partial credit.

Together, the episodes illustrate three properties of the logged WebShop process that matter for OPE. First, behavior-policy outputs can contain literal placeholders, repeated searches, and concatenated actions. Second, the policy’s reasoning text may disagree with its executed action and with the resulting environment reward. Third, WebShop returns multi-valued terminal rewards, whereas ALFWorld uses sparse binary success.

Graded rewards do not themselves cause the variance of IS-family estimators; that instability is driven primarily by products of behavior-to-evaluation policy ratios over long trajectories.

We selected Episode 2 for its short, directly verifiable partial-reward contrast. Episode 1 was selected because its horizon is close to the behavior pool average and because it exposes realistic logging and policy failures, rather than because it is a clean or unusually favorable trajectory. Both examples follow the same observation–action–reward schema used throughout the WebShop behavior pool.

F.12 Verified action-projection trace: ALFWorld

The WebShop examples above illustrate irregularities in an agent’s own outputs. ALFWorld exposes a complementary issue: the action stored in a trajectory can differ from the action text produced by the LLM because the collection pipeline projects malformed or inadmissible outputs onto the current admissible-command set. We verified the following trace against the exact step-level log, including its 29 recorded admissible_commands, and against the projection and repair logic of our data collection pipeline.

Step Executed action Effect
6 go to cabinet 1 Deterministic repair redirects the agent away from the garbage can.
7 go to garbagecan 1 The policy navigates back to the intended receptacle.
8 move apple 2 to garbagecan 1 The policy executes the task-progressing command and completes the task.

This trace clarifies which action an offline evaluator must model. The raw reasoning and ACTION: string define u6u_{6} and explain the policy’s intent, but the transition is generated by the projected action a6a_{6} stored in the trajectory. Thus, the relevant conditional is

P(o7,r6∣h6,a6=go to cabinet 1),P(o_{7},r_{6}\mid h_{6},\,a_{6}=\texttt{go to cabinet 1}),

not a transition conditioned on the unexecuted raw string go to garbagecan 1..

Our world-model training tuples use the projected action ata_{t} that was actually passed to the environment. The raw LLM response and utu_{t} are retained only as auxiliary logged text. Consequently, (ot+1,rt)(o_{t+1},r_{t}) is aligned with the executed action that generated it; the discrepancy illustrated here is not a transition-label error in Adwm’s training data. The same projection interface is applied during imagined evaluation-policy rollouts before the world model predicts the next latent state.

The trailing period contributes to the failed string normalization and to the token-overlap tie, but the more fundamental trigger is that the model proposes an action that is not admissible in the current state. The resulting detour is therefore neither environment stochasticity nor random replacement; it is a deterministic side effect of the collector’s admissible-action repair rule.

Appendix G Baseline Implementation Details

All baselines follow the COBS reference protocol of Voloshin et al. [36] unless stated otherwise. The full set of estimators is included in our released code.

G.1 Behavior log-probability extraction

For likelihood-based baselines, the distinction between raw LLM output utu_{t} and projected action ata_{t} matters. The exact probability of an executed action under an LLM-plus-projection system is

πΓ​(at∣ht)=∑uπ~​(u∣ht)​Γenv​(at∣ht,u,𝒜adm​(ht)),\pi_{\Gamma}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})=\sum_{u}\widetilde{\pi}(u\mid h_{t})\,\Gamma_{\mathrm{env}}\!\left(a_{t}\mid h_{t},u,\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{adm}}(h_{t})\right), (53)

which aggregates every raw output that the projection maps to ata_{t}. Enumerating this preimage is intractable for an open-vocabulary LLM.

Following the COBS-style implementation used by our likelihood baselines, we therefore score the canonical logged action string ata_{t} under the behavior and evaluation LLMs. We re-run each LLM in inference mode and extract token log-probabilities over that action span. Longest-common-token- prefix matching handles BPE merge boundaries between the prompt and action region. Let π¯b​(at∣ht)\bar{\pi}_{b}(a_{t}\mid h_{t}) and π¯e​(at∣ht)\bar{\pi}_{e}(a_{t}\mid h_{t}) denote these token-likelihood proxies. We apply ε\varepsilon-mixing at the probability level,

π¯eε​(at∣ht)=(1−ε)​π¯e​(at∣ht)+ε​𝕀[at∈𝒜adm(ht)]|𝒜adm​(ht)|,\bar{\pi}_{e}^{\varepsilon}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})=(1-\varepsilon)\bar{\pi}_{e}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})+\varepsilon\frac{\mathbb{I}[a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{adm}}(h_{t})]}{|\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{adm}}(h_{t})|},

and use

ρt=π¯eε​(at∣ht)π¯b​(at∣ht)\rho_{t}=\frac{\bar{\pi}_{e}^{\varepsilon}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})}{\bar{\pi}_{b}(a_{t}\mid h_{t})}

in IS, WIS, and DR.

Because the behavior data are generated with greedy decoding, these token likelihoods are also proxies for the probabilities of the deterministic behavior policy. These are proxy ratios over canonical action strings, not exact induced probability ratios from Eq. 53 when the projection is many-to-one. The ALFWorld trace in Section F.12 gives a concrete example of this gap. This limitation affects the likelihood-based baselines, not Adwm, which does not use importance ratios and conditions its transition model on the executed action ata_{t}.

G.2 Estimator formulas

For a logged trajectory τ=(s0,a0,r0,…,sT,aT,rT)\tau=(s_{0},a_{0},r_{0},\ldots,s_{T},a_{T},r_{T}), let ρt\rho_{t} denote the token-likelihood proxy ratio defined in Section G.1, with cumulative ratio ρ0:t=∏k=0tρk\rho_{0:t}=\prod_{k=0}^{t}\rho_{k} and discount γ=0.99\gamma=0.99:

J^DM\displaystyle\hat{J}^{\text{DM}} =1N​∑τ∑tγt​Rθ​(s^t)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\tau}\sum_{t}\gamma^{t}\,R_{\theta}(\hat{s}_{t}) (direct method, no ρ\rho) (54)
J^IS\displaystyle\hat{J}^{\text{IS}} =1N∑τρ0:T∑tγtrt,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\tau}\rho_{0:T}\!\sum_{t}\gamma^{t}r_{t},\quad J^WIS=∑τρ0:T∑tγtrt∑τρ0:T\displaystyle\hat{J}^{\text{WIS}}=\frac{\sum_{\tau}\rho_{0:T}\sum_{t}\gamma^{t}r_{t}}{\sum_{\tau}\rho_{0:T}} (55)
J^FQE\displaystyle\hat{J}^{\text{FQE}} =1N​∑τVπeε​(s0)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\tau}V_{\pi_{e}^{\varepsilon}}(s_{0}) (no per-trajectory ρ\rho) (56)
J^DR\displaystyle\hat{J}^{\text{DR}} =1N∑τ∑tγt[ρ0:trt+ρ0:t−1V(st)−ρ0:tQ(st,at)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\tau}\sum_{t}\gamma^{t}\!\left[\rho_{0:t}\,r_{t}+\rho_{0:t-1}V(s_{t})-\rho_{0:t}\,Q(s_{t},a_{t})\right] (57)

with the convention ρ−1=1/N\rho_{-1}=1/N for the COBS DR_v2 step-form. The DR network values VV and QQ are taken from the FQE Q-network. The baselines use γ=0.99\gamma=0.99 following COBS, whereas Adwm and the ground truth use the undiscounted episode score; since all methods are compared by Spearman ρ\rho across ε\varepsilon levels, only the ranking of each estimate matters.

G.3 Per-cell importance-ratio variance

Empirically observed cumulative log-ratio magnitudes at ε=0.5\varepsilon{=}0.5 span tens of nats per trajectory (HotpotQA up to ±24\pm 24, ScienceWorld ±18\pm 18, ALFWorld ±35\pm 35, WebShop ±28\pm 28), corresponding to per-trajectory ratios that span ∼16\sim 16–3030 orders of magnitude. This is the regime in which IS and DR estimates fluctuate by 102010^{20} or more even in double-precision arithmetic; our raw baseline output JSONs (released alongside the code) record DR values up to |JDR|≈×1020|J^{\text{DR}}|\!\approx\!6\!\times\!10^{20} on HotpotQA-PRM, exemplifying this divergence. The corresponding rank-correlations become driven entirely by floating-point underflow ties rather than the underlying signal.

G.4 FQE Q-network and per-ε\varepsilon correction

The FQE Q-network is a 2-hidden-layer MLP Qϕ:ℝdz+da→ℝQ_{\phi}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}+d_{a}}\!\to\!\mathbb{R} (dz+da→128→128→1d_{z}{+}d_{a}\to 128\to 128\to 1, SiLU activations). A target network Qϕ′Q_{\phi^{\prime}} is updated by Polyak averaging (ϕ′←0.99​ϕ′+0.01​ϕ\phi^{\prime}\leftarrow 0.99\,\phi^{\prime}+0.01\,\phi). optimization: Adam, lr ×10−43\!\times\!10^{-4}, batch size 64, 20 epochs, discount γ=0.99\gamma=0.99. Each training minibatch consists of (st,at,rt,st+1,donet)(s_{t},a_{t},r_{t},s_{t+1},\text{done}_{t}) tuples drawn from 𝒟b\mathcal{D}_{b}, and the Bellman target is y=rt+γ⁡(1−donet)​Vπeε​(st+1)y=r_{t}+\gamma\,(1-\text{done}_{t})\,V_{\pi_{e}^{\varepsilon}}(s_{t+1}) with Vπeε​(s)=(1−ε)​maxa​Qϕ′​(s,a)+ε​Q¯ϕ′​(s)V_{\pi_{e}^{\varepsilon}}(s)=(1{-}\varepsilon)\max_{a}Q_{\phi^{\prime}}(s,a)+\varepsilon\,\bar{Q}_{\phi^{\prime}}(s) where Q¯ϕ′​(s)\bar{Q}_{\phi^{\prime}}(s) is the action-mean across the admissible set. The maxa\max_{a} approximation is used because the LLM does not expose a full per-action probability vector. It evaluates the greedy policy with respect to Qϕ′Q_{\phi^{\prime}} rather than the action chosen by πe\pi_{e}, so FQE depends on πeε\pi_{e}^{\varepsilon} only through ε\varepsilon and the per-ε\varepsilon data filtering below; this is a limitation of FQE in the LLM-agent setting rather than of Adwm.

Per-ε\varepsilon correction.

Under the COBS protocol, mixing is applied at evaluation time as Vε​(s)=(1−ε)​maxa​Qϕ′​(s,a)+ε​Q¯ϕ′​(s)V_{\varepsilon}(s)=(1{-}\varepsilon)\max_{a}Q_{\phi^{\prime}}(s,a)+\varepsilon\,\bar{Q}_{\phi^{\prime}}(s), producing a value linear in ε\varepsilon and trivially monotonically decreasing. This artefact gives FQE a spurious ρ>0\rho{>}0 on the ε\varepsilon-axis even when its underlying state-value estimate is incorrect, and inflates the COBS-protocol headline number to a rank that has nothing to do with the policy being scored. We remove this artefact by training a separate Q-network for each ε\varepsilon level using πb\pi_{b} trajectories filtered against the ε\varepsilon-mixed behavior likelihood, then evaluating each on its own Vπeε​(s0)V_{\pi_{e}^{\varepsilon}}(s_{0}) at the trajectory start. This is the per-ε\varepsilon correction reported in the main text and is the only modification to FQE relative to COBS. Without it, FQE reports a near-uniform ρ=+0.9\rho{=}{+}0.9 on every cell; with it, the true rank correlation collapses or inverts as reported in Table 2.

Appendix H Additional Results

H.1 Per-seed Spearman ρ\rho

Table 5 reports the full 5-seed breakdown that underlies the avg-J^\hat{J} row of Table 2. Per-seed Spearman is computed by independently running each ε\varepsilon cell with seed si∈{0,1,2,3,4}s_{i}\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}, which propagates randomness through both imagined-rollout sampling and the ε\varepsilon-greedy admissible-action choice. The two reward-dense cells (HotpotQA-DPO, ScienceWorld-ETO) are highly stable across seeds (σ≈0.10\sigma\!\approx\!0.10); the ALFWorld and WebShop cells show larger per-seed variance because high-ε\varepsilon GT saturates near zero, making the 5-point Spearman ill-conditioned at the seed level. The avg-J^\hat{J} aggregator used in Table 2 mitigates this by averaging J^\hat{J} across seeds before computing ρ\rho.

H.2 Underlying J^\hat{J} and GT curves

Table 6 provides the seed-averaged J^\hat{J} values and ground-truth success curves underlying every row of Table 2, so that any of the reported correlations can be reproduced exactly.

H.3 Training loss and OPE accuracy

We also compared held-out denoising, reward, and termination losses with the downstream OPE error across world-model checkpoints. We found no consistent correlation between these losses and OPE accuracy. Fig. 3 therefore reflects optimization stability, while OPE accuracy is evaluated directly against ground-truth returns in Table 2 and Appendix H.

Appendix I Additional Ablations

I.1 Five-seed extension of Fig. 4

Figure 4 reports single-seed ρ\rho values to keep the component story compact. For each variant we also re-ran the full 5-seed protocol on the same three environments and recovered the same qualitative ordering: removing local CFG drops WebShop ρ\rho to +0.12±0.08+0.12\pm 0.08 across seeds, removing continuation guidance drops it to +0.27±0.10+0.27\pm 0.10, and removing the ψ\psi adapter drops HotpotQA to +0.42±0.07+0.42\pm 0.07. No 5-seed run flips the sign of the corresponding single-seed value, and the relative magnitude of each component’s contribution is preserved.

I.2 Latent capacity ablation

Beyond the inference-time guidance and adapter terms ablated in Fig. 4, we probe the latent capacity on WebShop, the most data-sensitive of our cells. Halving the latent dimension from dz=64d_{z}{=}64 to dz=32d_{z}{=}32 produces a complete inversion (ρ=−1.00\rho{=}-1.00), suggesting that the latent is at a representational floor below which contrastive features cannot be preserved. Adequate latent capacity must therefore be in place before any choice of guidance can recover positive ranking. We did not observe similar inversions on HotpotQA or ScienceWorld at the same cut, suggesting that the WebShop result reflects the combination of long-horizon search and continuous partial reward rather than a generic property.

I.3 ψ\psi-adapter loss design

Table 7 shows that the loss design we adopt (InfoNCE + ×0.1\!\times MSE) is essential. Pure MSE collapses to a near-constant adapter on every environment because per-token-mean target embeddings have low variance, providing the optimiser with no signal to differentiate latents; pure InfoNCE produces a discriminative adapter whose outputs drift out-of-distribution for the LLM and break its downstream input expectations. The combined loss outperforms either alone on all three environments.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  4. Justification: The abstract and introduction clearly state the three contributions (Theorem 1, guided diffusion realization, empirical evaluation), and the experimental results in Section 5 directly support these claims.

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

    Limitations

  7. Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: Section 6 and Appendix A discuss the limitations, including policy diversity, offline coverage, ranking versus calibration, cross-step error propagation, GT evaluation quality, and ψ\psi-adapter retraining when switching evaluation LLM families.

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.

    • •

      The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction).

  46. 10.

    Broader impacts

  47. Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

  48. Answer: [Yes]

  49. Justification: The framework reduces the need for live agent deployment during evaluation, lowering both API cost and the risk of irreversible side effects; no foreseeable negative societal impacts are identified beyond standard ML misuse concerns.

  50. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

    • •

      If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

    • •

      Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

    • •

      The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

    • •

      The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

    • •

      If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

  51. 11.

    Safeguards

  52. Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)?

  53. Answer: [N/A]

  54. Justification: The paper does not release new pretrained models or scraped datasets that pose misuse risk.

  55. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks.

    • •

      Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.

    • •

      Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.

    • •

      We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.

  56. 12.

    Licenses for existing assets

  57. Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected?

  58. Answer: [Yes]

  59. Justification: All benchmarks and LLM checkpoints used are cited with their original papers; publicly released checkpoints from prior work are listed in Table 1 with citations.

  60. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets.

    • •

      The authors should cite the original paper that produced the code package or dataset.

    • •

      The authors should state which version of the asset is used and, if possible, include a URL.

    • •

      The name of the license (e.g., CC-BY 4.0) should be included for each asset.

    • •

      For scraped data from a particular source (e.g., website), the copyright and terms of service of that source should be provided.

    • •

      If assets are released, the license, copyright information, and terms of use in the package should be provided. For popular datasets, paperswithcode.com/datasets has curated licenses for some datasets. Their licensing guide can help determine the license of a dataset.

    • •

      For existing datasets that are re-packaged, both the original license and the license of the derived asset (if it has changed) should be provided.

    • •

      If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators.

  61. 13.

    New assets

  62. Question: Are new assets introduced in the paper well documented and is the documentation provided alongside the assets?

  63. Answer: [Yes]

  64. Justification: The world model code and behavior trajectory pools are publicly released with usage instructions.

  65. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not release new assets.

    • •

      Researchers should communicate the details of the dataset/code/model as part of their submissions via structured templates. This includes details about training, license, limitations, etc.

    • •

      The paper should discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people whose asset is used.

    • •

      At submission time, remember to anonymize your assets (if applicable). You can either create an anonymized URL or include an anonymized zip file.

  66. 14.

    Crowdsourcing and research with human subjects

  67. Question: For crowdsourcing experiments and research with human subjects, does the paper include the full text of instructions given to participants and screenshots, if applicable, as well as details about compensation (if any)?

  68. Answer: [N/A]

  69. Justification: The paper does not involve crowdsourcing or human subject experiments.

  70. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper.

    • •

      According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector.

  71. 15.

    Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects

  72. Question: Does the paper describe potential risks incurred by study participants, whether such risks were disclosed to the subjects, and whether Institutional Review Board (IRB) approvals (or an equivalent approval/review based on the requirements of your country or institution) were obtained?

  73. Answer: [N/A]

  74. Justification: No human subjects are involved.

  75. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not involve crowdsourcing nor research with human subjects.

    • •

      Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper.

    • •

      We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution.

    • •

      For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review.

Note that if the LLM is used only for writing, editing, or formatting purposes and does not impact the core methodology, scientific rigor, or originality of the research, declaration is not required.

  78. Answer: [Yes]

  79. Justification: LLMs (πb\pi_{b} and πe\pi_{e}) are core components of the evaluation framework; their roles as behavior and evaluation policies are described throughout Sections 3–5.
